findings.paper_title: Progress report and interim audit findings - September 2026 - AC
findings.headline: The council is working through a formal multi-year Regaining Assurance program following the HRA ringfence breach, with oversight by MHCLG and PSAA.
findings.detail: A Regaining Assurance Strategy report was presented to the Audit Committee in June 2026, and an assessment of the timeline for rebuilding assurance was submitted to MHCLG and PSAA at the end of July. Auditors will continue to consider the nature, extent and likely timing of work required as the audit progresses. The audit is notably further progressed than at the equivalent point last year.
findings.matters: Formal involvement of MHCLG and PSAA indicates regulator oversight and a structured recovery plan, but the multi-year timeline signals that confidence in the council's financial control will not return swiftly.
findings.figures: June 2026 presentation; July 2026 submission to MHCLG and PSAA
findings.quote: We presented our Regaining Assurance Strategy report to the Authority's Audit Committee in June. We submitted our assessment of the likely timeline for the build back of assurance over the Authority's financial statements to MHCLG and PSAA at the end of July.

findings.paper_title: Progress report and interim audit findings - September 2026 - AC
findings.headline: Auditors have raised potentially significant queries on group consolidation financial information and group entities' accounting policies.
findings.detail: Auditors questioned the financial information used to set group audit strategy and have raised potentially significant queries on the data. An assessment of whether group organisations account for items under different frameworks (such as FRS 102 versus Code accounting) has not been provided despite being requested. This assessment is marked as a significant delivery risk (rating R) for the 30 November deadline.
findings.matters: If group entities are miscategorized or using inconsistent accounting policies, the consolidated financial statements could materially misstate the council's financial position.
findings.figures: 30 November 2026 deadline; risk rating R (significant risk of non-completion)
findings.quote: We have raised some potentially significant queries on the financial information on which this was based.

findings.paper_title: Progress report and interim audit findings - September 2026 - AC
findings.headline: Auditors have raised a specific query about the nature and accounting of the council's LOBO loans, complicating Financial Instruments audit work.
findings.detail: A separate query has been raised regarding the council's LOBO loans during the Financial Instruments audit. The report does not disclose what specific aspect prompted the query or what the council's response was, only noting that the query 'may further complicate the work in this area'. LOBO loans carry refinancing risk; auditors may be seeking clarity on accounting treatment, call dates, or terms.
findings.matters: LOBO loans create refinancing risk if lenders exercise call options; understanding their nature, terms and call dates is material to assessing the council's borrowing costs and liquidity.
findings.figures: Not specified in report
findings.quote: A separate query has been raised regarding the nature of the Authority's LOBO loans, as this may further complicate the work in this area.

findings.paper_title: Progress report and interim audit findings - September 2026 - AC
findings.headline: The finance team delayed delivery of audit information to prioritize meeting the 30 June statutory accounts deadline, pushing audit work back by several weeks.
findings.detail: Auditors originally planned to complete interim testing before receiving draft accounts, but the finance team did not provide required information on schedule, choosing instead to focus on the statutory deadline for publishing draft accounts. As a result interim audit work was delayed. At mid-audit, 15 information requests remained outstanding. Early performance shows only 25% of papers delivered by 5 June against a 100% target, 43% by 15 June, and 32% by 30 June.
findings.matters: Delayed audit extends the period during which lenders lack financial assurance. It also suggests structural tensions between statutory publishing requirements and audit cooperation.
findings.figures: 15 requests outstanding as of 15 September; 5 June – 25% (3/12), 15 June – 43% (3/7), 30 June – 32% (43/137)
findings.quote: The Authority did not provide the required information in line with the agreed timetable, as the finance team focussed their efforts on meeting the statutory deadline for publishing the draft financial statements.

findings.paper_title: Progress report and interim audit findings - September 2026 - AC
findings.headline: Control environment weaknesses from the HRA ringfence breach remain unresolved, with internal audit having done limited verification work in 2024/25 and 2025/26.
findings.detail: Auditors note that their risk assessment factors in historic weaknesses in the control environment identified by independent reviews following the HRA ringfence breach. Internal Audit has undertaken limited work in recent years on journal controls, authorisation limits, segregation of duties, and related areas. Audit testing has also identified 3 instances in payroll testing where supporting documentation for leavers is lacking.
findings.matters: Unresolved control weaknesses mean financial errors or irregularities could occur without detection, materially misstating the accounts.
findings.figures: 3 issues in payroll testing of leavers; limited work undertaken by Internal Audit in 2024/25 or 2025/26
findings.quote: Our risk assessment in this area factors in historic weaknesses in the control environment identified by independent reviews following the breach of the HRA ringfence in earlier years.

findings.paper_title: Progress report and interim audit findings - September 2026 - AC
findings.headline: Auditors will issue a disclaimer of opinion on the financial statements rather than a clean or qualified opinion.
findings.detail: Grant Thornton anticipates issuing a disclaimer of audit opinion by 30 November 2026. A disclaimer means the auditors cannot express an opinion on whether the financial statements are fairly presented. This follows a multi-year 'Regaining Assurance' program begun after the HRA ringfence breach. The council's draft accounts were delivered on time, but historic weaknesses in the control environment are still factoring into the audit risk assessment.
findings.matters: A disclaimer means lenders cannot rely on the financial statements for credit decisions and signals the council cannot demonstrate financial control adequate for conventional assurance.
findings.figures: 30 November 2026
findings.quote: We anticipate issuing a disclaimer of audit opinion by 30 November 2026, following the Audit Committee meeting on 27 November 2026.

findings.paper_title: Local Growth Fund Business Investment Fund
findings.headline: Council must mobilise 2.4-3 FTE staff within two weeks of approval, with delayed mobilisation risking programme clawback
findings.detail: The programme is approved for October 2026 start, requiring the council to recruit or redeploy 2.4 FTE staff immediately. The paper identifies as a specific risk that staffing may not be in place quickly enough to deliver programme administration within required timescales, which could trigger clawback. All staffing must be funded from the £567,000 fixed administration budget.
findings.matters: Staffing delays in grant administration could result in clawback of external funding. A lender needs to understand whether operational and staffing constraints could result in financial loss.
findings.figures: 2.4 FTE year 1; 3 FTE years 2-3; £567,000 fixed administration budget
findings.quote: Staffing capacity may not be in place quickly enough to mobilise the programme and deliver grant administration within the required timescales.

findings.paper_title: Local Growth Fund Business Investment Fund
findings.headline: Programme runs until 2030, crossing Local Government Reorganisation in April 2028, with funding transfer arrangements still to be determined
findings.detail: The Business Investment Fund operates October 2026 to March 2030. Local Government Reorganisation creates a new Greater Nottingham Council in April 2028. The paper states the council will work with EMCCA and the new authority to transfer the grant without impacting outputs, but the allocation process was still under consideration at report date.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand risks around programme continuity during structural change. Mishandled authority transfers or funding loss in transition could trigger clawback if new authorities fail to meet programme obligations.
findings.figures: £8,100,000 programme; October 2026 to March 2030 funding period; LGR effective April 2028
findings.quote: The current funding runs until 2030 and therefore will be impacted by LGR. At this stage the process of re-allocation of grant funding from existing authorities to the new authorities is under consideration by the relevant LGR workstream.

findings.paper_title: Local Growth Fund Business Investment Fund
findings.headline: Council carries clawback risk if Business Investment Fund is not properly managed
findings.detail: The council does not fund the scheme but bears delivery, compliance, audit, reputational and financial clawback risk if administration or grant recipients fail to meet terms. Clawback could arise from failure to comply with the Grant Funding Agreement, recipient failure to deliver outputs, or failure to achieve agreed outcomes.
findings.matters: A material contingent liability: if the council fails in its Accountable Body duties or recipients breach grant terms, the council may be required to repay part or all of the £8.1m from its own resources.
findings.figures: £8,100,000 contingent liability exposure; £567,000 administration budget from which mitigation costs must be funded
findings.quote: It should be noted that the Council is not funding the scheme from its own resources, but it does carry delivery, compliance, audit, reputational and potential clawback risk if the programme is not properly managed.

findings.paper_title: Local Growth Fund Business Investment Fund
findings.headline: Subsidy Control Act compliance responsibilities remain unresolved between council and EMCCA
findings.detail: The Grant Funding Agreement does not yet clarify whether the council or EMCCA will be responsible for subsidy control compliance, record-keeping, responding to investigations, indemnity or bearing the cost of any clawback. The paper lists seven unresolved areas requiring urgent clarification before any grants can be awarded without exposure to non-compliance and recovery action.
findings.matters: Unresolved compliance responsibilities create contingent liability. A lender needs to know whether the council could be exposed to clawback or regulatory enforcement for failures not within its control.
findings.figures: £8,100,000 at risk of clawback if subsidy control mechanisms fail
findings.quote: Depending upon the structure of the scheme, responsibility for subsidy control compliance may rest with EMCCA, the Council as Accountable Body, or both.

findings.paper_title: Local Growth Fund Business Investment Fund
findings.headline: Grant Funding Agreement not finalized before Council is asked to delegate authority to sign it
findings.detail: As of 15 September 2026, the Director of Legal Services had not received a detailed draft of the Grant Funding Agreement. The Executive Board is being asked to delegate authority to sign an agreement whose legal terms have not been reviewed, with review to happen after approval, subject to future acceptance of final terms.
findings.matters: A lender needs assurance that material funding agreements creating contingent liabilities have been properly reviewed by the council's legal team before execution. Signing without legal review is a governance red flag.
findings.figures: £8,100,000 funding
findings.quote: Unfortunately, a more detailed draft Grant Funding Agreement has not been shared with the Council at the time of publication of this report, meaning more definitive legal advice on its terms and any associated risks cannot be provided.

findings.paper_title: Cover Report - Adult Social Care Strategy - Enabling Gloriously Ordinary Lives
findings.headline: Strategy implementation is occurring during Local Government Reorganisation, requiring the strategy to 'remain adaptable through any LGR transition while maintaining continuity of improvement.'
findings.detail: Section 1.7 states that 'consideration will need to be given to how future organisational arrangements may affect operating models, workforce planning, commissioning, partnerships, governance, data, digital arrangements and system alignment.' The strategy's anticipated long-term efficiencies depend on successful delivery of multiple transformation programs (Improvement Plan, Target Operating Model, digital capability, commissioning) that must proceed during this organizational restructuring while the council remains under Department of Health scrutiny.
findings.matters: The council is delivering a complex multi-component transformation during organizational restructuring and ongoing regulatory scrutiny; disruption to implementation could prevent realization of anticipated financial benefits and increase budget pressure.
findings.figures: No delivery metrics or timelines provided; strategy explicitly states need for 'adaptability through any LGR transition.'
findings.quote: The strategy will therefore need to remain adaptable through any LGR transition, while maintaining continuity of improvement, statutory assurance and a clear focus on outcomes for people and communities.

findings.paper_title: Cover Report - Adult Social Care Strategy - Enabling Gloriously Ordinary Lives
findings.headline: The strategy commits to major service transformation from residential to home-based care models expected to create 'efficiencies over time,' but without quantified savings targets or financial modeling.
findings.detail: The finance partner states the shift 'will be better value for the authority in the long run and will benefit the people of Nottingham City.' However, section 5.2 confirms 'There are no direct financial implications from this decision at this time; however, the movement to a more preventative model of care could create efficiencies over time.' The council provides no financial analysis, savings targets, or implementation timelines despite declaring this a Key Decision.
findings.matters: The council expects long-term financial benefits from a major transformation but has not quantified expected savings or provided financial analysis, creating uncertainty about whether anticipated benefits will materialize and whether the transformation requires additional investment.
findings.figures: No savings targets or financial modeling provided; finance partner uses hedged language: 'could create efficiencies over time' and 'better value...in the long run.'
findings.quote: The move from a more traditional residential approach to Adult Social Care to a more home-based offer will be better value for the authority in the long run and will benefit the people of Nottingham City.

findings.paper_title: Cover Report - Adult Social Care Strategy - Enabling Gloriously Ordinary Lives
findings.headline: Adult Social Care received a CQC rating of Requires Improvement in 2025, with identified weaknesses in safe pathways, systems, governance, and sustainability.
findings.detail: The CQC assessment found 'significantly weaker areas relating to safe pathways, systems and transitions, and governance, management and sustainability' (section 1.3). This triggered additional Department of Health and Social Care scrutiny. An Adult Social Care Improvement Plan was developed as 'a single, coordinated programme of change to respond to the CQC findings and additional Department of Health and Social Care scrutiny.'
findings.matters: A regulatory downgrade and identified governance/sustainability weaknesses reduce council credibility and increase organizational risk, constraining the council's autonomy and decision-making authority.
findings.figures: CQC overall rating: Requires Improvement (2025); significant weaknesses identified in safe pathways, systems and transitions, and governance and sustainability.
findings.quote: In 2025, Adult Social Care was assessed by the Care Quality Commission and received an overall rating of Requires Improvement. The assessment identified significantly weaker areas relating to safe pathways, systems and transitions, and governance, management and sustainability.

findings.headline: PWLB debt maturity profile is well-distributed with only 1.12% due within 12 months, reducing refinancing risk.
findings.detail: The largest proportion of PWLB debt (33.85%) matures within 5 to 10 years, with 35.96% maturing between 25 and 40 years. Only 1.12% is due within the next 12 months, well below the 25% upper limit set in the Treasury Strategy. This distribution smooths refinancing demand across time.
findings.matters: Lenders care about refinancing risk; a concentrated short-term maturity profile creates future funding pressure, while a distributed profile demonstrates prudent debt management.
findings.figures: 1.12% due within 12 months; 33.85% matures in 5-10 years; 35.96% matures in 25-40 years; 25% upper limit
findings.quote: Only 1.12% of borrowing matures within the next 12 months, helping to reduce refinancing risk.

findings.headline: Council temporarily breached its Treasury Management Strategy counterparty limits during Q1 but corrected the position in July.
findings.detail: During Q1, the council held investment balances with counterparties above its approved threshold for longer than the four-day tolerance specified in its Treasury Management Strategy. The paper describes this as 'prudent from a treasury management perspective' but notes it was 'a departure from the approved strategy'. The position was corrected in July 2026 by redistributing the investment portfolio.
findings.matters: Adherence to approved treasury controls and strategy matters to lenders as an indicator of governance discipline; a temporary breach followed by swift correction demonstrates risk management oversight.
findings.figures: four-day allowance exceeded
findings.quote: During the quarter ended 30 June, the Council departed from its own pre-set counterparty limit by holding balances above the target threshold for longer than the four-day allowance set out in the Treasury Management Strategy.

findings.headline: Council repaid £24.3m of external debt in Q1 with no new long-term borrowing undertaken.
findings.detail: External loans debt decreased by £24.3m, comprising £9.3m of PWLB repayment and £15m of market loan repayment. The council undertook no new long-term borrowing during the quarter, indicating active debt reduction rather than refinancing need.
findings.matters: Lenders track whether councils are reducing debt burdens or becoming more leveraged; active debt repayment signals improved financial position.
findings.figures: £24.3m total reduction (£9.3m PWLB, £15m market loans); no new borrowing
findings.quote: No new long-term borrowing has been undertaken in the first quarter of 2026/27, the balance of external loans debt has decreased by £24.3m with the repayment of £9.3m of PWLB and £15m of market loans.

findings.paper_title: Local Growth Fund Skills and Employment
findings.headline: £1.188m employment programme must continue through Local Government Reorganisation, creating transition risk
findings.detail: The programme runs until March 2029, overlapping with LGR. The council acknowledges that accountable body responsibilities, grant compliance, delivery partner agreements, audit records and any potential clawback liabilities must be considered in transition planning, with arrangements documented and capable of transfer to successor authority.
findings.matters: A lender needs assurance that financial commitments survive structural change. Failure to transition cleanly could result in service disruption, audit findings or clawback liability.
findings.figures: programme runs until 31 March 2029
findings.quote: There are no immediate Local Government Reorganisation implications, but as the programme runs to March 2029, accountable body responsibilities, grant compliance, data-sharing arrangements, delivery partner agreements, audit records and any potential clawback liabilities will need to be considered as part of future LGR transition planning

findings.paper_title: Local Growth Fund Skills and Employment
findings.headline: Council accepts £1.188m Local Growth Fund grant with clawback liability for delivery partner underperformance
findings.detail: The council is accepting up to £1.188m from EMCCA to deliver an employment support programme. As accountable body, the council receives the grant, administers it, and remains liable for clawback if delivery partners fail to achieve performance targets. The grant is fully ringfenced and does not create General Fund pressure.
findings.matters: This is external income that benefits the council without General Fund pressure, but creates a contingent liability if delivery targets are not met. A lender needs visibility of grant administration risks and conditional liabilities.
findings.quote: Clawback remains the responsibility of NCC as the recipient of the funds.

findings.paper_title: Enc. 2 for Adult Social Care Strategy - Enabling Gloriously Ordinary Lives
findings.headline: Council's own engagement identified financial constraint and reduced capacity as core barriers to delivering its Adult Social Care strategy.
findings.detail: Nottingham's engagement process explicitly identified that "the core risk to delivery is the gap between ambition and operational reality." Stakeholders highlighted tension between the strategy's ambitions and the "current climate of financial constraint and reduced capacity to deliver." Staff expressed significant concerns about the council's capacity to realise the strategy's ambitions. The strategy requires substantial resource investment for redesign and capacity building, but neither costs nor funding sources have been identified or quantified.
findings.matters: A lender needs to assess whether a council can realistically deliver its stated commitments. If staff and stakeholders doubt capacity due to financial constraint, this signals either unmet funding needs, risk of underperformance against strategy, or the need to revise ambitions to match available resources.
findings.figures: 530 staff members engaged across 7 sessions, 203 community members across 15 groups, 178 survey responses
findings.quote: There is a tension perceived between the ambitions of the strategy and the current climate of financial constraint and reduced capacity to deliver.

findings.paper_title: Essential Health & Safety Works – Community Assets
findings.headline: Full Repairing and Insuring leases will transfer building maintenance liabilities from council to community organizations, removing ongoing subsidy
findings.detail: Under FRI leases, community organizations will assume future repair, maintenance and statutory compliance responsibilities. This removes ongoing Council subsidies and shifts contingent maintenance liabilities to occupiers, improving the council's long-term financial position if organizations remain solvent and occupied.
findings.matters: Successful liability transfer reduces long-term council obligations; however, organization failure or vacancy could force the council to resume holding and maintenance costs unexpectedly
findings.figures: Remaining £0.300m subsidy to be removed
findings.quote: remove the remaining £0.300m subsidy and reduce ongoing Council liabilities.

findings.paper_title: Essential Health & Safety Works – Community Assets
findings.headline: Risk register identifies multiple factors that could prevent delivery of the £300k MTFP saving; fallback mitigations not detailed
findings.detail: The paper documents explicit risks to delivery including associations unwilling to accept future liabilities and procurement delays. The risk register notes that wider financial mitigations have been negotiated if the MTFP saving is not delivered, but does not specify what these are, when they would apply, or their scale.
findings.matters: Contingent savings plans require credible mitigation strategy; vague reference to unspecified financial fallbacks creates uncertainty about the council's ability to manage non-delivery
findings.figures: £0.300m MTFP saving at risk
findings.quote: put delivery of the remaining £0.300m Medium Term Financial Plan saving for community centres at risk.

findings.paper_title: Essential Health & Safety Works – Community Assets
findings.headline: £300k earmarked reserves designated to cover non-capitalizable costs of the asset transition
findings.detail: The council holds £300k in earmarked reserves funded from revenue to cover transition costs that do not qualify for capital treatment. This will be drawn on for ineligible expenditure, subject to Section 151 officer approval, reducing the reserves available for other pressures.
findings.matters: Shows planned reserve depletion and indicates some transition costs will be treated as revenue; signals either underfunded capital allocation or costs ineligible for capital treatment
findings.figures: £300k earmarked reserves
findings.quote: the Council holds earmarked reserves of £300k, funded from revenue resources to cover ineligible capital expenditure, subject to approval of the Section 151 officer.

findings.paper_title: Essential Health & Safety Works – Community Assets
findings.headline: Capital investment amount not disclosed; commercially sensitive appendix withholds budget being committed to achieve £300k saving
findings.detail: The council is seeking approval for capital funding for repairs and statutory compliance works to enable the asset transition, but the specific amount is excluded from the paper as commercially sensitive. This prevents assessment of whether the capital being committed represents value for the £300k saving being targeted.
findings.matters: A lender assessing value for money needs to see the capital-to-saving ratio; withholding the investment amount prevents evaluation of financial proportionality
findings.figures: Capital amount withheld in Appendix 1 (exempt)
findings.quote: The value of the funding is contained in Appendix 1, which is an exempt item in this report.

findings.paper_title: Essential Health & Safety Works – Community Assets
findings.headline: £604k MTFP savings already removed from 2024/25 and 2025/26 budgets, with £300k contingent on completing asset transition
findings.detail: The council has already assumed £604k of recurring savings in its budgets for 2024/25 and 2025/26, pending implementation of Full Repairing and Insuring leases. Of this, £300k remains to be delivered. If the transition does not complete—associations unwilling to sign leases, delivery delays, or lease negotiations failing—these budgeted savings will not materialize.
findings.matters: A lender assessing financial sustainability needs to know whether budgeted savings will materialize; savings dependent on complex organizational change carry explicit delivery risk
findings.figures: £0.604m applied to 2024/25 and 2025/26 revenue budgets; £0.300m remaining to be delivered
findings.quote: The MTFP savings of £0.604m have been applied to the 2024/25 and 2025/26 revenue budgets, ahead of the implementation of the new operating lease arrangements outlined in this report.

findings.headline: Nationally funded schemes via accountable body underspent by £14.898m – Warm Homes and Decarbonisation programmes not deployed
findings.detail: Three accountable body schemes show significant underspends: Warm Homes Social Housing Fund (£7.018m), Warm Homes Local Grant (£4.641m), and Social Housing Decarbonisation Fund Wave 2 (£3.239m). These are funds where the council administers national government programmes.
findings.matters: Undeployed grant funding carries clawback risk, suggests governance or delivery issues with national scheme administration, and may affect the council's standing with government for future funding allocations.
findings.figures: (14.898)m total accountable body variance comprising (7.018)m, (4.641)m, and (3.239)m
findings.quote: Accountable Body MNZH - Warm Homes Social Housing Fund (7.018) MNZH - Warm Homes Local Grant (4.641) CAP- MNZH Social Housing Decarbonisation Fund Wave 2 (3.239) Subtotal: Accountable Body (14.898)

findings.headline: Capital programme forecast to underspend by £38.775m in 2026/27 based on Q1 trends
findings.detail: The council's capital programme shows a forecast full-year underspend of £38.775m based on Q1 variances. Major underspends include CERS schemes (£15.590m), accountable body schemes (£14.898m), and Growth & City Development (£3.968m).
findings.matters: A significant shortfall in capital programme delivery could indicate programme management issues, slippage in planned investments, or scope changes that affect borrowing requirements and council financial forecasts.
findings.figures: (38.775)m total variance; (15.590)m CERS; (14.898)m accountable body; (3.968)m Growth & City Development
findings.quote: Capital Programme Variances - Q1 (38.775)

findings.headline: £16.6m of savings targets brought forward from previous years remain undelivered, with the pattern expected to continue into 2027/28
findings.detail: The council is carrying forward £16.596m of undelivered savings targets from prior years. In Q1 2026/27, only 90% of these prior-year targets are on track to deliver, with £4.298m at risk (26%) and £1.734m (10%) forecast as non-delivery. The council forecasts £1.269m of 2026/27 savings will slip into 2027/28 and £1.678m will not be delivered at all, indicating the savings shortfall is structural rather than temporary.
findings.matters: A multi-year pattern of unmet savings targets suggests structural budget pressures that the council may be unable to resolve through service changes alone, potentially requiring persistent reserve drawdown or refinancing of existing debt
findings.figures: Undelivered savings brought forward £16.596m; 2026/27 delivery rate 90%; at risk £4.298m; non-delivery £1.734m. 2027/28 forecast: £1.269m slipped to next year, £1.678m recurrent non-delivery
findings.quote: This table summarises performance against the undelivered savings brought forward from prior years.

findings.headline: £13.7m (36%) of £37.9m 2026/27 savings targets are at risk of not being delivered, with only £9.4m (25%) confirmed as delivered
findings.detail: As of Q1 2026/27, only £9.431m of required savings have been delivered (blue). A further £14.799m (39%) are on track (green), but £10.711m (28%) are at risk (yellow) and £2.947m (8%) are forecast as non-delivery (red). The Adult Social Care and Health directorate is performing worst at 82% delivery versus the council average of 92%, suggesting particular pressure in the largest budget area.
findings.matters: If at-risk and non-delivery savings of £13.7m do not materialise, the council will face an equivalent budget shortfall requiring either reserve drawdown or additional spending cuts mid-year
findings.figures: Total savings required £37.888m; delivered £9.431m; on track £14.799m; at risk £10.711m; non-delivery £2.947m. ASC&H total required £11.664m with 82% delivery rate
findings.quote: This table summarises performance against the approved 2026/27 savings (new and previously agreed saving increases) as well the undelivered savings brought forward from prior years.

findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account capital spending reduced by £17.1m in Q1, driven primarily by £11.9m of carry-forward work from 2025/26 being reprofiled to future years.
findings.detail: The HRA directorate experienced a net reduction of £17.1m in Q1 amendments. The largest component is work originally planned to complete in 2025/26 and subsequently in 2026/27 now being pushed to future years (£11.9m). Additional reductions include Energy Efficiency & Tackling Fuel Poverty (£2.6m), schemes pending business case approval (£2.6m), Building a Better Nottingham (£0.8m), and Decent Neighbourhoods (£0.5m).
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether £11.9m of housing investment is being deferred due to funding constraints, delivery problems, or other issues, and whether the scaling back of energy efficiency programmes indicates broader constraints on the housing capital plan.
findings.figures: HRA total movement: (£17.123m); carry forwards reprofiled: (£11.937m); Energy Efficiency reduction: (£2.551m); schemes pending approval: (£2.605m)
findings.quote: 25/26 carry forwards reprofiled to future years (11.937)

findings.headline: Council repaid £24.3m of borrowing in Q1 and does not expect to borrow further, keeping debt reduction on track.
findings.detail: During Q1 2026/27, the council reduced borrowing by £24.3m. Treasury management activity remained prudent and compliant with Prudential Indicators, prioritising security and liquidity. In line with the Treasury Management Strategy, the council does not expect to borrow in 2026/27. Any additional borrowing would incur revenue financing costs affecting the budget.
findings.matters: Debt reduction is financially positive and signals the council is improving its balance sheet position. A lender views this favourably as it reduces leverage and improves financial headroom.
findings.figures: Borrowing reduction Q1: £24.3m
findings.quote: borrowing reduced by £24.3m during the quarter, and all treasury activity remained within approved limits.

findings.headline: Capital programme increased by £49m to £282.7m, mostly from prior-year slippage of £41.5m being re-profiled.
findings.detail: The original 2026/27 capital budget of £233.7m increased by £49m, of which £41.5m is carry-forward from 2025/26 due to slippage. Q1 forecast shows £38.8m of the revised budget will not be spent this year, being re-profiled to future years. Largest variance is in CERS (£15.6m) mainly from highways and vehicle replacement programme delays. The council is working to reprofile the 2025/26 carry-forward.
findings.matters: Repeated capital slippage can signal delivery capacity constraints or project governance issues. However, this also affects cash flow and may free resources. A lender examining capital delivery track record and future funding would note the re-profiling.
findings.figures: Original 2026/27 budget: £233.7m; revised budget after carry-forward and approvals: £282.7m; Q1 forecast: £243.9m; forecast underspend: £38.8m
findings.quote: The 2026/27 Capital Programme has increased by £49.0m since the original approved budget due to carry forward from 2025/26 for slippage in activity (£41.5m) and new projects approved (£7.5m).

findings.headline: Cross-cutting workforce savings of £10m+ across council are only partially delivered, creating unplanned overspends held at directorate level.
findings.detail: The council set cross-cutting workforce savings targets totalling approximately £10m across directorates (Adult Services £3m, CERS £3.8m, Finance & Resources £3m, Growth & City Development balance). As of Q1, these are only partly delivered. For example, CERS has delivered £0.7m of its £3.8m target, leaving £1.3m at risk. These unallocated savings are creating directorate-level budget pressures that are being partially offset by staff vacancies and planned underspends.
findings.matters: Workforce savings across a large organisation signal financial stress and cost-cutting. If the council cannot execute these without creating service gaps or relying on recruitment freeze to offset, this suggests either the savings are unaffordable or that delivery will cause service quality degradation.
findings.figures: Adult Services: £3m unallocated workforce savings; CERS: £3.8m with £1.3m at risk; Finance & Resources: £3m to be met through vacant post deletion; total cross-cutting workforce component approximately £10m+
findings.quote: Of the £3.8m cross-cutting workforce savings, the directorate has plans to deliver £0.7m. Further work is being undertaken to identify mitigations for the full savings target (the £1.3m At Risk) through vacancy management and additional income in year.

findings.headline: Adult Social Care £4.1m overspend driven by external care package demand outpacing budget, partly offset by reserve releases.
findings.detail: Adults & Public Health is forecast to overspend by £4.1m, primarily from £6.2m overspend on external care packages in Access & Prevention, of which £2.1m relates to undelivered savings. The council is partly mitigating through £1.4m reserve release for transformation costs and £0.5m assumed mitigation against undelivered savings. The service is developing a recovery plan. This reflects ongoing capacity and demand pressures from an ageing population and increasing complexity of needs.
findings.matters: This is a recurring directorate overspend and signals that demographics and service demand are creating a structural deficit in adult social care. Use of reserves to offset operational overspends reduces financial flexibility.
findings.figures: £4.1m directorate overspend; £6.2m external care package overspend; £2.1m from undelivered savings; £1.4m reserve release; £0.5m assumed mitigation
findings.quote: £6.2m overspend on external care package expenditure. £2.1m of this relates to undelivered savings (relating to both new 2026/27 savings and undelivered savings brought forward from prior years).

findings.headline: General Fund unallocated reserves falling to 6% of net expenditure, below the 10% minimum recommended by the Section 151 Officer.
findings.detail: The council's minimum recommended reserve balance is 10% of net expenditure (£41.99m). Due to the £15.2m provision made for the DSG High Needs deficit and other reserve movements, the unallocated General Fund balance will fall to 6% (£26.4m). The Section 151 Officer notes this position will be recalibrated as DSG implications become known, but the current forecast leaves the council below its own stated prudent minimum.
findings.matters: A lender assesses financial resilience partly by the size of useable reserves. Falling below the council's own minimum threshold indicates reduced flexibility to absorb further shocks and increased financial fragility.
findings.figures: Minimum recommended: 10% of £419.9m net expenditure = £41.99m; forecast closing balance: 6% = £26.4m
findings.quote: Due to the provision made for the DSG deficit as outlined above, the unallocated General Fund financial reserves balance will reduce to 6% of the current 2026/27 net expenditure budget of £419.9m.

findings.headline: Nearly £3m of budgeted savings not on track to deliver, requiring urgent mitigation.
findings.detail: The council budgeted £21.3m of new 2026/27 savings and £16.6m of prior-year carried-forward savings. Only £20.1m (94%) and £14.9m (90%) are forecast to deliver respectively, leaving £1.2m and £1.7m without robust delivery plans. These failures require urgent mitigation to prevent them falling to the bottom line. The position assumes some at-risk savings (£6.4m) will be delivered in full.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether management can execute the savings on which the budget was built. Recurring failure to deliver signals that the underlying budget is unaffordable and that forecasts may be optimistic.
findings.figures: £21.3m new savings approved, £20.1m (94%) forecast to deliver, £1.2m (6%) at risk; £16.6m brought forward, £14.9m (90%) forecast to deliver, £1.7m (10%) at risk
findings.quote: Currently £20.1m (94%) of the new 2026/27 savings are forecast to be delivered in 2026/27, with £1.2m (6%) of savings remaining without robust delivery plans.

findings.headline: High Needs Block forecasting £27.3m in-year deficit, £24.2m worse than planned recovery.
findings.detail: The Dedicated Schools Grant High Needs (SEND) Block is forecasting a £27.3m deficit, driven by demand exceeding forecasts. This would fully deplete the £12.1m reserve and create a cumulative deficit of £15.2m. Worst case is £31.3m deficit. The service is undertaking a fundamental review and rebasing of the recovery plan. Critically, the statutory override protecting the council from this liability ceases 31 March 2028, after which the accounting treatment is uncertain and any deficit would need funding from the General Fund.
findings.matters: A lender assessing the council's financial sustainability must understand that a material unfunded liability is building that will impact the General Fund from 2028 onwards unless the council closes the gap or government provides additional funding.
findings.figures: £27.3m in-year deficit; £12.1m reserve; £15.2m cumulative deficit by 31 March 2027; worst case £31.3m; statutory override ends 31 March 2028
findings.quote: The High Needs (SEND) Block is forecasting an in year deficit of £27.3m, £24.2m adverse to the assumptions underpinning the approved DSG Recovery Plan, largely due to unforeseen and unrelenting demand increases exceeding original forecasts.

findings.committee: East Midlands Shared Services Joint Committee
findings.headline: EMSS operational reserves fully depleted; partnership now has no financial buffer against overspends
findings.detail: EMSS had historically maintained reserves for redundancy costs, invest-to-save initiatives, and exceptional operational demand. The Joint Committee approved removal of these reserves in June 2022 when they fell below best practice. The balance has now been fully depleted. Going forward, Nottingham City Council and Leicestershire County Council must fund any operational overspend on a 50:50 basis with no contingency available.
findings.matters: Nottingham City's financial resilience is affected by its reliance on EMSS; the elimination of reserves means unexpected operational costs must now be funded immediately from the council's own budget rather than from partnership contingencies
findings.figures: Reserve balance now £0; NCC contribution to EMSS £3.226 million (55.45% of £5.818 million partnership funding)
findings.quote: The balance of reserve has now been fully depleted and partners will be expected to fund any operational overspend arising in year on a 50:50 basis.

findings.paper_title: 2. Motion in the name of Cllr Kirsty L Jones - Cease the use of Bailiffs for Families with Children and to Review Practices of Council Tax Debt Collection in Nottingham
findings.headline: Bailiff enforcement extracts high costs that consume collection proceeds, leaving only 27p per £1 for the council.
findings.detail: Bailiff fees and administrative costs are substantial. A 2018 Freedom of Information request found that councils recover only 27p net from every £1 referred to bailiffs, meaning 73% of the enforcement cost is absorbed by bailiff fees and administration rather than reaching the council.
findings.matters: The council is using a revenue collection method where three-quarters of the enforcement cost evaporates; this represents financial inefficiency in managing a critical revenue stream and suggests alternative collection methods might be more cost-effective.
findings.figures: 27p per £1 referred
findings.quote: A 2018 Freedom of Information request showed that for every £1 referred to bailiffs for collection, councils only received 27p.

findings.paper_title: 2. Motion in the name of Cllr Kirsty L Jones - Cease the use of Bailiffs for Families with Children and to Review Practices of Council Tax Debt Collection in Nottingham
findings.headline: Council tax bailiff referrals surged 34% in one year while collection recovery remains weak.
findings.detail: Bailiff referrals rose from 17,361 cases in 2024/25 to 23,294 in 2025/26. Nationally, bailiffs recovered only £255.8m of £755.3m referred in 2025 (34% recovery). Nottingham's historical experience is worse: in 2014/15, only £2.2m was recovered from £9.2m referred (24% recovery).
findings.matters: Council tax is a primary revenue stream; rising enforcement referrals despite low recovery rates suggests collection is deteriorating and the council is relying on an ineffective mechanism to cover a growing collection gap.
findings.figures: 2024/25: 17,361 cases; 2025/26: 23,294 cases (34% increase); nationally 2025: £255.8m recovered of £755.3m referred; Nottingham 2014/15: £2.2m recovered of £9.2m referred
findings.quote: In 2024/25, Nottingham City Council referred 17,361 cases of council tax arrears for enforcement action. In 2025/26, this number had risen to 23,294.

findings.headline: Nottingham's Council Tax collection rates are significantly below comparators, and a proposed policy change would worsen this weakness
findings.detail: The S151 Officer states that collection rates are already significantly lower than comparable authorities. A motion to eliminate bailiff enforcement (the final enforcement tool) would further compromise this position and negatively impact the council's finances and service viability.
findings.matters: Council Tax is material revenue; weakness here directly threatens financial viability and service delivery, and any policy narrowing collection options is a material risk
findings.figures: collection rates significantly lower than comparable authorities
findings.quote: Nottingham City Council's collection rates are already significantly lower than comparable authorities. The inability to use Bailiffs would only compromise this position further. The elimination of Baillifs as a last resort measure will negatively impact the City's finances and will in turn pose a threat to the future financial viability of key services

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation presents substantial unknown risk to audit and financial governance position
findings.detail: The Council is due to be replaced by a larger local authority through LGR by 2028/29. External auditors and management acknowledge that the impacts of this restructuring on the audit position are not currently known. The Audit Committee explicitly noted LGR as representing a substantial area of risk.
findings.matters: Fundamental structural change creates uncertainty about how financial accountability and audit will be managed post-reorganisation, affecting the trajectory of audit assurance recovery.
findings.figures: LGR anticipated by 2028/29; spans period when audit disclaimed opinions are expected
findings.quote: Fundamentally, it is not known what that the impacts of LGR will be on the Council's audit position at the current time. The Committee noted, therefore, that LGR represents a substantial area of risk.

findings.headline: Staff churn and control gaps: Internal audit upgraded from Limited to Moderate Assurance but with consistency and resilience concerns
findings.detail: Internal Audit opinion improved to Moderate Assurance (from Limited in 2024/25), but auditors found controls are not consistently applied across the organisation. Staff churn has created single points of failure risk, and succession planning is needed to embed recent control improvements and ensure long-term resilience.
findings.matters: Governance resilience is at risk if key staff leave; control inconsistencies could undermine financial reporting reliability.
findings.figures: Opinion upgraded from Limited Assurance (2024/25) to Moderate Assurance (2025/26)
findings.quote: churn in staff has emphasised risks around potential single points of failure, which should be mitigated against

findings.headline: External audit will issue disclaimed opinions for years due to unaudited historic period from Coronavirus pandemic
findings.detail: Disclaimed audit opinions are anticipated until after the 2027/28 audit because of an unaudited historic period in the Council's accounts from 2019/20 onwards. The external auditor cannot fill this gap within available capacity. The Council maintains its accounts are accurate and it holds sufficient reserves, but external audit assurance remains qualified.
findings.matters: A lender cannot obtain full external audit verification of the Council's financial position for at least two more years, relying instead on management assurance and disclaimed opinions.
findings.figures: Disclaimed opinions anticipated through 2027/28 audit; materiality threshold £1.2 million
findings.quote: it is anticipated that disclaimed opinions will be made until after the 2027/28 audit

findings.headline: Accounts Payable authorization failures persist despite S114 spending controls introduced in 2023
findings.detail: Following the Section 151 Officer's 2023 S114(3) report, Accounts Payable audit found continuing issues: vacation rule authorisations being misdirected and payments authorised by officers lacking appropriate delegation authority. No PO No Pay policy implemented June 2025 has reduced but not eliminated Retrospective Purchase Orders. Audit confirms S114 controls have not adversely affected payment timeliness but underlying authorization weaknesses remain.
findings.matters: Continuing payment authorization failures despite prior S114 intervention indicate persistent governance weakness; unauthorized payments represent ongoing financial control risk to the council.
findings.figures: Continuing vacation rule issues; Retrospective Purchase Orders still being required despite No PO No Pay policy implementation
findings.quote: Payments are being authorised by officers who do not have the appropriate levels of authorisation.

findings.headline: Accounts Receivable collection has deteriorated with 45.1% of debt over one year old
findings.detail: Accounts Receivable audit found 45.1% of total outstanding debt aged over 1 year, indicating ongoing recovery challenges. Substantial element relates to Adult Social Care land charges where recovery is uncertain and dependent on asset realisation. Some long-standing debts are beyond statutory recovery period, increasing unrecoverable income risk. Audit notes 'further review of aged debt is required to ensure debts with no realistic prospect of recovery are identified and written off in a timely manner.'
findings.matters: Aged debt at this level indicates deteriorated cash flow collection and represents material unrecovered income; debts beyond statutory recovery represent write-off risk and uncollectable assets on balance sheet.
findings.figures: 45.1% of total outstanding debt aged over 1 year; substantial proportion relates to Adult Social Care land charges
findings.quote: 45.1% total outstanding debt aged > 1 year, indicating ongoing recovery challenges.

findings.headline: Salary overpayments remain at £540k with no reduction despite new monitoring systems
findings.detail: Salary overpayments audit found persistent high levels totalling £540k (November 2025) with no reduction in occurrence. Weaknesses include weak policy compliance, extended recovery periods without proper approval, capacity constraints in Legal Services delaying recovery, inconsistencies between Legal and financial records, no central write-off register, and limited escalation to senior management. Root causes (late manager notifications) not effectively addressed despite new Power BI dashboard.
findings.matters: Persistent unrecovered overpayments of this scale indicate fundamental control weaknesses in a critical payroll function; lack of reduction despite new controls suggests the improvements are not addressing underlying causes.
findings.figures: £540k outstanding as of November 2025; one significant case of £20k highlighting ongoing weaknesses
findings.quote: High and persistent level of overpayments (As at November 2025, £540k outstanding) with no reduction in occurrence.

findings.headline: Direct Payments scheme (£18.9m budget) has control weaknesses with emerging financial and safeguarding risks
findings.detail: Direct Payments audit found approval arrangements inconsistent with Scheme of Delegation, limited segregation of duties with key responsibilities in single roles, over-reliance on small number of officers, and incomplete assurance over managed account provider (which lost FCA registration). Financial monitoring not completed quarterly due to resource constraints. Audit identified: 'Emerging financial and safeguarding risks... including accounts with no recorded payments, increasing personal contribution deficits, potential misuse of funds, and unresolved investigations.' Notes that despite compliance improvements, 'increasing contribution deficits and accounts with no recorded payments suggest a deterioration in some key financial and safeguarding risk areas.'
findings.matters: Weaknesses in a £18.9m scheme carrying direct financial and safeguarding risks, with identified deterioration in financial outcomes and over-reliance on individuals, expose the council to significant loss and regulatory action.
findings.figures: £18.9m Direct Payments budget; increasing contribution deficits; accounts with no recorded payments
findings.quote: Emerging financial and safeguarding risks were identified, including accounts with no recorded payments, increasing personal contribution deficits, potential misuse of funds, and unresolved investigations.

findings.headline: Capital Works Programme governance has significant weaknesses limiting effectiveness of control framework
findings.detail: Audit of the council's capital programme identified multiple control failures: lack of formal escalation mechanism for project variances, absence of formal year-end capital outturn review, single-point dependency in capital project financial oversight, limited budget oversight without formal documentation, and reduced lessons learned activities. The audit concludes the framework 'could become inadequate and ineffective in supporting the governance and successful delivery of the capital programme unless the identified improvements are implemented.'
findings.matters: Capital programme governance weaknesses directly impair the council's ability to deliver infrastructure commitments and manage capital borrowing effectively, affecting financial resilience and creditworthiness.
findings.figures: Not specified; identified across capital works governance
findings.quote: Despite the existence of a centralised governance framework and established oversight arrangements, the audit identified weaknesses that collectively significantly reduce the effectiveness, consistency and resilience of capital programme governance.

The Council's financial resilience is dependent on delivery of the Transformation Programme savings, maintaining financial discipline across services, and stable funding assumptions.
findings.matters: The Council has just emerged from a Section 114 notice and the AGS is flagging that recovery remains fragile and contingent on specific management actions.

findings.headline: Financial forecasting accuracy is weak, evidenced by a massive gap between Exceptional Financial Support approved and actually required.
findings.detail: The 2024/25 budget included £41.024m of Exceptional Financial Support, but only £7.737m was required at year-end—a £33.3m forecasting error. This suggests the Council's budget planning and demand forecasting is unreliable.
findings.matters: A lender relies on forecasts of financial need, savings delivery and budget performance. A forecast error of this scale indicates material forecasting weaknesses.

findings.headline: External Audit has identified 'significant weaknesses across all three VfM criteria for the fifth consecutive year', indicating systemic governance, financial management and efficiency failures.
findings.detail: Grant Thornton's 2024/25 Value for Money assessment identified significant weaknesses in financial sustainability, governance, and economy/efficiency/effectiveness. Key issues include weaknesses in budget setting assumptions, delivery and transparency of savings, immature risk management, limitations in internal audit effectiveness, and ongoing challenges in procurement, ICT governance, and service improvement in Housing, Adults and Children's Services. Three new recommendations raised in 2024/25 with prior-year recommendations still in progress.
findings.matters: A five-year trend of VfM weaknesses across all three criteria suggests the Council's ability to deliver value for money and manage its operations effectively remains fundamentally constrained.
findings.figures: Five consecutive years (2020/21–2024/25) of significant VfM weaknesses identified; three new recommendations in 2024/25
findings.quote: identified significant weaknesses across all three VfM criteria—financial sustainability, governance, and improving economy, efficiency and effectiveness—for the fifth consecutive year

findings.detail: The Head of Internal Audit concluded that whilst key elements of governance, risk management and control framework are in place, their inconsistent application and varying levels of maturity limit overall effectiveness. Audit findings identified that controls are not yet fully embedded in some areas, particularly where processes rely on manual intervention, data quality is variable, or governance arrangements are still maturing.
findings.matters: Moderate assurance is a weak verdict and means financial processing, budget control, and governance processes cannot be relied upon to operate consistently.
findings.figures: Moderate assurance opinion for 2025/26; response rate on effectiveness survey 51.6% (16 of 31 senior officers)
findings.quote: For 2025/26, the opinion is moderate assurance, reflecting that, whilst key elements of the governance, risk management, and control framework are in place, their inconsistent application and varying levels of maturity limit overall effectiveness.

findings.paper_title: Enc. 1 for Draft Annual Governance Statement 2025 - 2026
findings.headline: Adult Social Care has been issued a Section 50 notification by the Department of Health and Social Care for failing to meet statutory duties under the Care Act.
findings.detail: The Care Quality Commission assessment (December 2025, published June 2026) concluded Adult Social Care 'requires improvement' and identified weaknesses in system safety, ineffective risk management, delays in assessments and reviews, and fragmented service delivery. Performance on key measures including timeliness of assessments remains below regional and national comparators. The Section 50 notification requires the Council to demonstrate remedial action to the Secretary of State.
findings.matters: A regulatory notification for non-compliance with statutory duties on a major demand-led service indicates systemic operational and governance failure that will consume management attention and may require significant additional investment.
findings.figures: CQC assessment December 2025; performance below regional and national comparators on Adult Social Care Outcomes Framework measures
findings.quote: Nottingham City Council has been issued with a Section 50 notification identifying areas where it is not meeting its statutory duties under the Care Act. The Council is therefore required to demonstrate remedial action to the Secretary of State for the Department of Health and Social Care.

findings.paper_title: Enc. 1 for Draft Annual Governance Statement 2025 - 2026
findings.headline: Council issued a Section 114 notice in November 2023 for inability to set a balanced budget; recovery is now early-stage despite achievement of 2026/27 balanced budget without Exceptional Financial Support.
findings.detail: Following a Section 114 notice issued by the then Section 151 Officer due to concerns about financial sustainability, Government appointed Commissioners to oversee recovery. The Council has since improved financial management, reduced reliance on Exceptional Financial Support (only £7.737m used of £41.024m approved in 2024/25), and set a balanced budget for 2026/27. However, the Commissioners' oversight concluded in March 2026, marking the start of the Council managing recovery independently.
findings.matters: Section 114 is a critical threshold event for local authority lending. While recovery progress is welcome, it is very early-stage and dependent on continued financial discipline.
findings.figures: Section 114 issued November 2023; Commissioners oversight concluded March 2026; EFS £41.024m approved 2024/25, only £7.737m required year-end; 2026/27 balanced budget achieved without EFS
findings.quote: In November 2023, a Section 114 (Part 3) report was issued to Councillors due to concerns regarding the financial sustainability of the Council

findings.detail: Grant Thornton has disclaimed audit opinions on the 2024/25 and previous five years' accounts, meaning auditors could not gain sufficient assurance to sign off the financial statements. The Council is undertaking an External Audit improvement programme to restore assurance over accounts and key balances, including reserves, but this work is not yet complete.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management 202526 Annual Report for Chair briefing

findings.detail: The council's own Treasury Management risk register shows a score of 4.23 against a target of 2.94—persistently above acceptable levels. The council acknowledges that 'there are still some improvements that can be made to reduce the risk to target', indicating known weaknesses in treasury controls that have not yet been remediated.
findings.matters: A lender financing local government borrowing needs confidence in the council's treasury risk management. An acknowledged gap between actual and target risk score, with unresolved improvement actions, suggests treasury controls are weaker than they should be and may require tighter monitoring.
findings.figures: Risk rating 4.23 (actual) vs target 2.94; likelihood categorised as 'unlikely' with 'minor' impact, but score is above the target 'remote/minor' threshold

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management 202526 Annual Report for Chair briefing
findings.headline: HRA debt-to-revenue ratio deteriorated significantly against budget
findings.detail: The Housing Revenue Account's debt-to-revenue ratio came in at 1.520 against an estimate of 1.050, a variance of 45% worse than forecast. This suggests either the estimate was poor or actual debt repayment/revenue collection did not perform as anticipated. The absolute debt levels did improve (£199.5m actual vs £263m estimate), so the deterioration is driven by lower-than-expected HRA revenue.
findings.matters: HRA sustainability depends on the balance between debt levels and revenue collection. A significant miss in this ratio signals either forecasting weakness or unexpected revenue shortfall in the housing business, both of which affect long-term HRA affordability and the council's ability to service housing debt.
findings.figures: HRA debt £199.5m (against estimate £263.0m), HRA revenues £130.9m (against estimate £130.3m), resulting ratio 1.520 actual vs 1.050 estimate
findings.quote: Ratio of Debt to Revenues 1.050 [estimate] 1.520 [actual]

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management 202526 Annual Report for Chair briefing
findings.headline: Council breached its own Treasury Management Strategy counterparty limits
findings.detail: The council held balances above the approved Lloyds Bank counterparty threshold for longer than the four-day allowance permitted in the Treasury Management Strategy Statement. This was done to support debt repayment activity and maintain liquidity during 'heightened uncertainty', but represents an explicit departure from the approved strategy that the council is transparently reporting.
findings.matters: A lender assessing control strength needs to know when a council departs from its own approved controls, even if management claims it was prudent. This indicates either the strategy was too rigid, or controls were not tight enough to enforce in practice.
findings.figures: The breach involved holding balances above the target threshold for an unspecified period longer than four days; the document does not quantify the excess held or for how long.
findings.quote: During the year, the Council departed from its own pre-set Lloyds Bank counterparty limit by holding balances above the target threshold for longer than the four-day allowance set out in the Treasury Management Strategy Statement.

findings.paper_url: https://committee.nottinghamcity.gov.uk/documents/s183978/Treasury Management 202526 Annual Report for Chair briefing.pdf
findings.headline: Investment balances declined 28% year-on-year while council relies on £603m internal borrowing
findings.detail: The council held £253.7m in investments at year-end, down from £351.1m (a £97.4m or 28% decrease). This mirrors the council's deliberate strategy of using £603.2m of internal borrowing to fund 44% of its capital financing requirement, avoiding external debt. The council forecasts balances will remain adequate, but the rate of decline may constrain future flexibility.
findings.matters: The council's ability to continue its debt reduction strategy without external borrowing is dependent on maintaining sufficient cash reserves; if balances continue to decline at current rates, the council may face pressure to take external borrowing at less favorable rates or adjust its capital program.
findings.figures: Investments £253.7m (2025/26) vs £351.1m (2024/25), a decline of £97.4m; internal borrowing £603.2m funds 44% of capital financing requirement of £1,153.0m
findings.quote: The Council's internal borrowing position at 31 March 2026 was £603.2m. This meant that approximately 44% of the overall capital borrowing need was not funded with loan debt as cash held by the Council for reserves, balances and cash flow was used as a temporary measure.

findings.headline: Tree Services overspend of £0.8m reflects costs of bringing service into legal compliance following safety incident, with ongoing budget pressure
findings.detail: Following a significant tree safety incident at Wollaton Park in 2024, the council implemented a comprehensive tree safety review and new inspection regime. Compliance costs resulted in an £0.8m overspend in 2025/26 for required maintenance and remedial works, and this is flagged as an ongoing pressure.
findings.matters: This reveals deferred maintenance liability that has now crystallised into a budget pressure. The council now carries heightened legal and reputational risk if tree safety standards slip again.
findings.figures: £0.8m overspend on Tree Services in year
findings.quote: A comprehensive review of Tree Services was undertaken in 2024 following a significant tree safety incident at Wollaton Park. This has resulted in a strengthened approach to tree safety management across Highways and Parks, including the implementation of a new Tree Safety Policy and an enhanced inspection regime. While these improvements have brought the service into a legally compliant position, they have also identified a substantial increase in required maintenance and remedial works, resulting in an ongoing budget pressure.

findings.headline: Corporate budget underspend of £34.6m is driven by one-off treasury gains (early debt repayment, investment income) not recurring in future years
findings.detail: The £34.6m underspend in corporate budgets is substantially composed of non-recurring items: £8.5m from early debt repayment discounts, £13.7m from higher treasury investment income, and £7.3m net release of insurance reserves. These mask the true underlying position and will not repeat.
findings.matters: The council's reported underspend relies heavily on one-off financial engineering and windfalls. Removal of these items from future years creates a material budget gap not yet addressed in the medium-term plan.
findings.figures: £8.5m debt repayment savings, £13.7m treasury gains, £7.3m insurance provision release, £34.6m total corporate underspend
findings.quote: Treasury and Capital Financing is underspent by £16.3m. This is mainly due to reduced borrowing costs as a result of a debt restructure exercise optimising interest rate shifts involving a significant repayment of legacy debt with available cash investments.

findings.headline: Savings programme delivering only 80%, with £5.6m at outright risk and future MTFP increasing targets by £5.3m
findings.detail: Of £39.1m approved savings, only £31.1m (80%) were delivered in 2025/26. £6.9m slipped to 2026/27 and £5.6m remain undelivered. The £10.2m workforce savings achieved were largely unplanned, through vacancy management and turnover rather than structured restructuring. Future years will require an additional £5.3m of workforce savings on top of carryforward undelivered targets.
findings.matters: Savings delivery shortfall in year is offset by in-year underspends but signals the council cannot reliably hit targets. Future years stack undelivered savings on top of new ones, compounding the risk of budget failure.
findings.figures: £31.1m delivered of £39.1m target (80%), £6.9m amber/delayed, £5.6m red/at risk, £10.2m achieved via vacancy only
findings.quote: £31.1m (80%) has been delivered in 2025/26, with £6.9m of slippage expected to be delivered in 2026/27 and £5.6m of non-delivered savings programmes. It is to be noted that although the £10.2m cross-cutting workforce savings have been delivered in 2025/26, this is largely via untargeted vacancy management and general turnover.

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant High Needs reserves depleting unsustainably, with deficit now £3.9m and recovery plan paused
findings.detail: The High Needs block shows a £3.9m deficit. Reserves have fallen sharply from over £21m two years ago to £12.1m now. The council acknowledges this trajectory is not sustainable and projects full depletion within four years without intervention. The DSG High Needs Recovery Plan was developed but then paused pending a national SEND White Paper.
findings.matters: A ringfenced grant deficit that is growing despite intervention signals unmanageable demand pressure. The pause on the recovery plan means no active mitigation is underway, and SEND costs are driven by statutory obligations the council cannot refuse.
findings.figures: £3.9m deficit, reserves £12.1m (down from £21m+), four-year depletion projection
findings.quote: While reserves remain sufficient to cover the in-year deficit of £3.9m, they have reduced materially over the past two years - from over £21m to £12.1m following the 2025/26 outturn. This position is not sustainable. Without intervention, current projections indicate that the deficit will continue to grow over the next four years, fully depleting reserves and potentially resulting in a significant cumulative deficit.

findings.headline: Adult Social Care overspend growing despite falling caseloads, with £9.9m provision for ICB income loss
findings.detail: The Adults and Public Health directorate reports an £11.6m overspend against £89.8m budget. The council has established a £9.9m provision against potential income reduction from the Integrated Care Board, reflecting a contested funding dispute. Despite reducing the number of care packages, average care costs per package continue to rise.
findings.matters: This reveals a structural cost pressure in a statutory service that is not being controlled by volume reductions. The ICB dispute is unresolved and represents contingent liability.
findings.figures: £11.6m overspend, £9.9m ICB provision, £10.7m savings target with only £5.5m delivered (52%)
findings.quote: The overspend includes the prudent recognition of a £9.9m provision in relation to the potential reduction of income due to the new ICB approach for jointly funded care packages. This represents the worst-case scenario; it is not an acceptance of liability. Dispute resolution is ongoing.

findings.headline: EMSS reserve fully depleted with no buffer for operational costs or unexpected pressures
findings.detail: The EMSS held reserves historically for redundancy costs, invest-to-save initiatives and exceptional demand. DfE Intervention Notice triggered sector-led improvement support. Children's Partnership Improvement Board established with DfE independent chair. findings.detail: Following Section 114, Secretary of State issued Directions on 22 February 2024 and appointed Commissioners. Council developed three-aim Improvement Plan covering financial sustainability, governance, and people/processes. Commissioners report positive progress but specifically advised 'over the coming year the Council will need to move into the implementation phase for these plans to have the required impact'. Implementation delivery is critical to financial recovery.

The Commissioners also advised that over the coming year; the Council will need to move into the implementation phase for these plans to have the required impact.

findings.detail: The Head of Internal Audit's opinion for 2024/25 is 'Limited assurance' on the adequacy and effectiveness of the control environment. findings.detail: Grant Thornton were unable by the statutory deadline to gain the requisite level of assurance on the 2023/24 Accounts and therefore disclaimed them entirely. Only the Value for Money Audit was completed. This is more serious than a qualified audit opinion and prevents reliance on audited financial statements for that year.

findings.figures: 2023/24 financial year
findings.quote: the 2023/24 Accounts were disclaimed as the auditors were unable by the backstop date to gain the requisite level of assurance on the Accounts. However, they were able to complete the Value for Money Audit. This was reported to the Audit Committee in March 2025.

findings.headline: Council required £41m exceptional financial support to set 2024/25 budget and remains under indefinite spending controls
findings.detail: A Section 114 report was issued in November 2023 when the council could not meet its statutory obligation to deliver a balanced budget. The government approved £41.024m of Exceptional Financial Support to 'capitalise' revenue expenditure. By year-end only £7.737m was drawn, but spend control policy has been extended indefinitely from its original March 2025 end date.
findings.matters: Direct evidence of financial crisis and ongoing dependency on exceptional measures; indefinite spending restrictions signal persistent concerns about financial discipline and management

findings.quote: In November 2023, a Section 114 (part 3) report was issued to Councillors due to the financial sustainability of the Council in line with the Local Government Finance Act 1988. The report was for the then Section 151 Officer to formally notify the Council that, in his professional opinion, the Council was unable to meet its statutory requirement to deliver a balanced budget for 2024/25.

findings.headline: Procurement compliance worsening: exemptions doubled to £20.34m value in one year, £9.278m avoidable
findings.detail: Procurement exemptions increased from 44 requested/33 approved in 2023/24 to 60 requested/54 approved in 2024/25. The total value of exemptions requested for 2024/25 was £20.34m, of which the council estimated £9.278m was avoidable. About 20 waivers occurred because of delays in compliant procurement processes.
findings.matters: Rising exemptions signal breakdown in procurement discipline and compliance. Avoidable exemptions suggest the council is not managing commercial processes properly, risking overpayment and non-competitive procurement.
findings.figures: 2023/24: 44 exemptions requested, 33 approved; 2024/25: 60 requested, 54 approved. Value of exemptions requested 2024/25: £20.34 million; avoidable portion: £9.278 million.
findings.quote: The number of procurement exemptions increased between 2023/24 and 2024/25 from 44 requested / 33 approved, to 60 requested / 54 approved. For 2024/25, the total value of exemptions requested was £20.34 million. Within this, the Council estimated that £9.278 million was avoidable.

findings.paper_title: External Audit Findings report 2024/25 and Value for Money report
findings.headline: Exceptional Financial Support massively overestimated: requested £41.143m for 2024/25, used only £7.737m
findings.detail: The government agreed to advance £41.143m in Exceptional Financial Support for 2024/25 based on the council's forecast. By August 2025, the council estimated it needed only £7.737m—a gap of £33.4m. This reversal indicates the original budget crisis was overstated or resolved faster than expected, but it also shows the council's inability to forecast its own position.
findings.matters: The council drew down far less government support than it anticipated, suggesting either the crisis was misunderstood or the recovery was unexpectedly rapid. Either way, it signals unreliability in the council's financial forecasting to government.
findings.figures: Government agreed-in-principle EFS for 2024/25: £41.143 million; estimated usage by August 2025: £7.737 million; gap: £33.406 million.
findings.quote: In February 2024, the Government confirmed that it was minded to approve the Council's request for EFS of £41.143 million in respect of 2024/25. In February 2025, the Government agreed-in-principle to further EFS requested by the Council of £25 million in respect of 2025/26 and £10 million in respect of 2026/27. By August 2025, the Council was estimating that only £7.737 million of the agreed-in-principal amount for 2024/25 had been needed; less than £10 million was needed in respect of 2025/26; and that nothing would be needed in respect of 2026/27.
