findings.detail: The council commissioned its first stock condition survey in a decade and identified that repairs and maintenance costs of £958 million will be needed over a rolling programme to bring housing stock up to standard. A regulatory notice from the Regulator for Social Housing remains active. Tenant satisfaction at end-Q2 2025/26 was 63%, lower than the 67% seen at start of 2023/24 (though recovering from 56% at end of 2023/24).
findings.matters: A £958m maintenance backlog is a massive unfunded liability. The council will need to borrow or find grants to address it, and service quality is affecting tenant confidence.
findings.figures: £958 million repairs and maintenance costs needed over rolling programme; tenant satisfaction 63% (Q2 2025/26), down from 67% (start 2023/24), up from 56% (end 2023/24).
findings.quote: the Council carried out its first stock condition survey for ten years and identified that repairs and maintenance costs of some £958 million will be needed over a rolling programme to bring the stock up to expected standards.

findings.paper_title: External Audit Findings report 2024/25 and Value for Money report
findings.headline: ICT systems in crisis: no strategy, unknown spend, no business cases, 86 improvement items identified
findings.detail: An independent review in March 2025 found the council's ICT function had no discernible strategy, no business cases, weak asset controls, unapproved cloud application access, and low staff morale. The review made 86 recommendations. The council cannot reliably state its annual ICT spend, estimated at £14.5–16 million. A new permanent Chief Technology Officer was recruited in September 2025 and took post in December 2025.
findings.matters: ICT system failures affect data integrity, operational continuity, and the reliability of all financial and operational information the council produces. Unknown spend and lack of controls are serious governance gaps.
findings.figures: 86 recommendations for improvement; estimated annual ICT spend £14.5–16 million (actual amount unknown); new Head of ICT recruited September 2025, posted December 2025.
findings.quote: business cases were not used for the ICT service; and control over ICT assets and services was weak. The review made 86 recommendations for improvement and noted that there was low morale within the ICT team.

findings.paper_title: External Audit Findings report 2024/25 and Value for Money report
findings.headline: Internal control environment broken: Internal Audit ignored, risk management in infancy, Strategic Risk Register inadequate
findings.detail: The Commissioners found that 'Internal Audit is largely ignored, its reports and recommendations have not been acted on for some time, resulting in a questionable internal control environment.' The Strategic Risk Register is not comprehensive or up to date. Risk management is in its infancy. In April 2025, there were 28 high-priority and 25 medium-priority Internal Audit recommendations outstanding, falling to 13 high and 15 medium by September 2025—but even these reductions are unvalidated.
findings.matters: A questionable internal control environment means risks are not being identified or managed. Controls over expenditure, fraud prevention, and operational reliability are compromised.
findings.figures: April 2025: 28 high-priority and 25 medium-priority audit recommendations outstanding. September 2025: 13 high-priority and 15 medium-priority (unvalidated reduction).
findings.quote: Internal Audit is largely ignored, its reports and recommendations have not been acted on for some time, resulting in a questionable internal control environment. Risk management is in its infancy, although some areas are better than others.

findings.paper_title: External Audit Findings report 2024/25 and Value for Money report
findings.headline: Accounts unaudited for five years; 2024/25 audit incomplete; reserves without external assurance since 2019
findings.detail: Accounts for 2019/20 through 2023/24 all received disclaimed opinions under government backstop arrangements. The 2024/25 audit remains incomplete at the time of this report. Reserves balances—a complex area that includes corrections from an HRA ringfence breach—have had no external audit assurance for five years. The council missed the 2024/25 accounts publication deadline by 11 days.
findings.matters: A lender cannot trust the council's financial position when accounts have gone unaudited for five years. Reserves cannot be verified, and corrections made after the HRA breach remain unaudited. This is a fundamental accountability gap.
findings.figures: Five consecutive years of disclaimed audit opinions (2019/20–2023/24); 2024/25 audit incomplete; accounts publication deadline missed by 11 days.
findings.quote: Under the Government's backstop arrangements, opinions were disclaimed on the accounts for all years inclusive from 2019/20 to 2023/24. The Council's existing systems, processes, and resources have not been sufficient to support the delivery of the 2024/25 external audit, and our audit of the financial statements remains incomplete.

findings.paper_title: External Audit Findings report 2024/25 and Value for Money report
findings.headline: Savings delivery masked by accounting: 85% target met but actual delivery obscured by employee budget 'cushion'
findings.detail: The council planned £42.398m in savings for 2024/25 and reported delivering £35.974m (85%). However, some planned savings didn't materialize. The shortfall was offset by not holding back budgets for staff vacancies—the Commissioners found 'full budgeting for the establishment posts with very little held back in terms of inevitable vacancies.' This masking means actual savings performance is worse than reported.
findings.matters: If reported savings aren't real, the council's financial position is worse than stated. Undelivered savings from prior years are also being re-profiled forward, compounding the problem.
findings.figures: Planned savings: £42.398 million; delivered: £35.974 million (85%). Transformation savings included £3.109 million rolled over from earlier years due to prior non-delivery.
findings.quote: Commissioners reported to the Secretary of State in August 2025 that, with regard to 2024/25, the 'shortfall was offset by some very significant 'savings' in the employee budget line. In reality, these savings were due to full budgeting for the establishment posts with very little held back in terms of inevitable vacancies.'

findings.paper_title: External Audit Findings report 2024/25 and Value for Money report
findings.headline: Budget forecasts wildly inaccurate: £171.7m deficit became £4.3m surplus after revisions mid-year
findings.detail: The original 2024/25 budget, published March 2024, forecast a £171.7m medium-term deficit. By October 2025, revised forecasts showed a £4.3m surplus—a swing of £176m. The 2025/26 budget gap fell from £68.957m to £20.793m. The council attributes the errors to unrealistic assumptions in the original budget, requiring major revisions over the course of the year.
findings.matters: Forecasting this poor is a core governance failure and makes financial planning unreliable. A lender needs confidence the council understands its actual position; this audit shows it didn't.
findings.figures: Original forecast deficit: £171.730 million; revised forecast surplus: £4.287 million. Original 2025/26 gap: £68.957 million; revised: £20.793 million.
findings.quote: The Council's view is that the original 2024/25 budget, developed during 2023/24 and published in March 2024, was underpinned by assumptions that have since proved to be unrealistic.

findings.headline: Access to financial data restricted to limited individuals, creating dependencies and operational risk.
findings.detail: Financial and transactional data access is restricted to a limited number of individuals across multiple systems, creating dependencies on specific personnel. Absences due to annual leave and sickness have resulted in delays obtaining critical information. The auditors note this creates operational risk as key data may be inaccessible during critical periods and may indicate loss of corporate knowledge.
findings.matters: Restricted access to financial systems indicates weak segregation of duties and creates fraud risk. Dependencies on individuals rather than systems mean financial information becomes unavailable when people are absent, threatening business continuity.
findings.figures: Issue identified across multiple systems
findings.quote: In addition, access to financial and transactional data is restricted to a limited number of individuals, creating dependencies on specific personnel. This issue has arisen across multiple systems, not just the Council's main general ledger. Absences due to annual leave and sickness have resulted in delays in obtaining critical information or passing it through central finance for validation before submission to the audit team. These constraints not only impact timeliness and efficiency but also introduces operational risk, as key data may be inaccessible during critical periods.

findings.headline: Unlawful HRA ringfencing breach from 2021 remains unresolved; cannot confirm if management override.
findings.detail: In December 2021 the Interim Chief Finance Officer issued a s114 notice after discovering the council had unlawfully breached the ringfencing requirement for the Housing Revenue Account over seven years, including 2019/20, 2020/21 and 2021/22. Five years later, auditors still cannot establish whether management override of controls caused this breach or whether other similar instances could have occurred.
findings.matters: An unresolved breach of legal ringfencing requirements, combined with inability to determine if it was caused by override or systematic weakness, indicates either weak controls or management misconduct. Either way it suggests past financial statements may be unreliable.
findings.figures: Seven-year breach period including 2019/20, 2020/21, 2021/22; s114 notice issued December 2021
findings.quote: In December 2021, the then Interim Chief Finance Officer issued a s114 notice after discovering that the Council had unlawfully breached the ring-fencing requirement for the Housing Revenue Account (HRA) over a period of seven years, including the 2019/20, 2020/21 and 2021/22 financial years.

findings.headline: Significant VFM weaknesses across all three criteria; auditors not satisfied council has proper arrangements.
findings.detail: Auditors identified significant weaknesses in the council's arrangements for improving economy, efficiency and effectiveness; financial sustainability; and governance. The auditors concluded they are not satisfied the council has made proper arrangements for securing economy, efficiency and effectiveness in its use of resources for 2024/25.
findings.matters: A formal finding that the council lacks proper arrangements for economy, efficiency and effectiveness questions whether it can be trusted to spend borrowed money wisely or manage its finances prudently.
findings.figures: Significant weaknesses in all three VFM criteria areas
findings.quote: We identified significant weaknesses in the Council's arrangements across all three specified criteria. We are therefore not satisfied that the Council has made proper arrangements for securing economy, efficiency and effectiveness in its use of resources for the financial year under review.

findings.headline: Management override of controls risk remains unresolved; auditors unable to obtain assurance it is absent.
findings.detail: The auditors were unable to obtain sufficient assurance that management override of controls is absent from the financial statements. This follows the same concern from prior years. They were unable to complete planned procedures to understand what actions the council has taken to address control environment issues previously identified, including the unlawful HRA ringfencing breach and high error volumes.
findings.matters: Management override of controls is a fundamental fraud risk. The council's inability or unwillingness to demonstrate controls prevent override indicates weak governance. This directly affects whether the accounts can be trusted.
findings.figures: Issue present continuously since 2019/20 audit
findings.quote: We have been unable to obtain sufficient assurance that management override of controls is absent within the financial statements. Due to the material and pervasive nature of the issue, we intend to continue to report this matter in the disclaimer of opinion.

findings.headline: £122.5m dwelling rents income and other material balances lack system support.
findings.detail: The council has been unable to provide detailed supporting listings from its core financial system or subsidiary systems for material balances. A significant example is £122.5m of dwelling rents income, which auditors were unable to commence work on pending an appropriate report. Other unsupported balances include £3.5m enforcement receivables and £2.9m managing agent property charges receivables.
findings.matters: Material income balances without system-generated supporting documentation indicate weak financial systems or data integrity issues. This creates operational risk and prevents verification of the council's asset and revenue position.
findings.figures: Dwelling rents £122.5m, enforcement receivables £3.5m, managing agent charges £2.9m
findings.quote: There are material balances and adjustments within the financial statements for which the Council has been unable to provide detailed supporting listings from its core financial system or supporting subsidiary systems. A significant example is the £122.5 million of income relating to dwelling rents, which we have been unable to commence work on, pending the provision of an appropriate report.

findings.headline: £10m income adjustments in March 2025 lack sufficient supporting evidence.
findings.detail: The council processed approximately £10m of adjustments increasing income and debtors at year-end, with the largest being a £6.129m HRA rental income adjustment in March 2025 to correct an imbalance in the housing rents system. The auditors state they were unable to gain sufficient appropriate assurance over the year-end balances and cannot confirm the adjustments were the appropriate corrections.
findings.matters: Unexplained, unsupported material adjustments at year-end raise fraud and accounting accuracy risks. A lender cannot trust the revenue line without evidence these corrections are valid.
findings.figures: £10m total adjustments, of which £6.129m HRA rental income
findings.quote: The Council has processed adjustments of approximately £10m which increase income and debtors. The largest of these adjustments was posted in March 2025 to correct an imbalance between the housing rents system arrears and the balance in the Council's balance sheet. This had the effect of increasing HRA rental income by £6.129m in 2024/25. We have been informed that these transactions were made following a review of the balance sheet as at 31 March 2025, however in each instance we have not been able to gain sufficient, appropriate assurance over the year-end balance.

findings.headline: Audit unable to complete work in any area of the 2024/25 accounts.
findings.detail: Audit fieldwork commenced July 2025 but the auditors have been unable to conclude their work in any area. They report that as of March 2026, their substantive audit findings are extremely limited, primarily due to lack of progress. Multiple areas lack key information, responses to significant queries have not been received, and critical evidence remains outstanding despite efforts by the council's finance team.
findings.matters: An audit unable to conclude on ANY balance means the financial statements cannot be relied upon for lending decisions or performance assessment. The council's true financial position is unknown.
findings.figures: Audit commenced July 2025, unable to conclude by March 2026 backstop date
findings.quote: Our audit fieldwork commenced in July 2025. We have been unable to conclude our audit work in any area of the accounts.

findings.headline: Dramatic recovery from financial crisis, but future years depend on savings assumptions not yet detailed
findings.detail: Projected MTFP deficit halved from £171m (March 2024/25 MTFP) to £37m; exceptional funding support dropped from £41m projected need to £7.8m actual in 2024/25; 2025/26 Q3 forecast shows £1m surplus and 2026/27 budget projects same. Officer states 'trajectory of improvement...can be fully sustained' but this assumes new savings will be introduced 2027/28-2029/30 as part of normal budget setting.
findings.matters: The recovery is genuine and impressive, demonstrating changed management capability; but the MTFP only balances to 2026/27 if future years' savings materialize, creating execution dependency that extends into years not yet detailed.
findings.figures: Deficit £171m to £37m; EFS need £41m to £7.8m actual; £1m General Fund surplus projected both 2025/26 and 2026/27
findings.quote: In 2024, the Council projected a funding gap requirement of £41m to be met by Exceptional Financial Support for 2024/25 but only required £7.8m. The 2025/26 forecast outturn as at Quarter 3 currently assumes no requirement for EFS and against a budget gap set of £20.8m, the Council will fully eliminate such a gap and record a surplus of £1m by 31 March 2026.

findings.headline: £28m earmarked for Local Government Reorganisation creates uncertain reserve exposure
findings.detail: Earmarked reserves include £28m provision for estimated LGR transitional costs, allocated from what was previously unallocated reserves. If LGR proceeds and costs exceed this estimate, additional funds would have to come from unallocated reserves already at statutory minimum.
findings.matters: LGR is a major structural change with uncertain costs; cost overruns would directly erode already-tight reserves, forcing either policy breach or further savings acceleration.
findings.figures: £28m LGR provision; earmarked reserves £188.3m of which this is material allocation
findings.quote: Given the likely LGR transitional cost liabilities estimated by advisers as £28m, such an allocation of 'unallocated' reserve is considered to be prudent.

findings.headline: Officer's positive approval is conditional on council stopping use of reserves to cover recurring revenue spending
findings.detail: The Section 151 Officer explicitly conditions his robust opinion on the council not calling on reserves to meet ongoing service costs or growth, only for identified risks. This indicates past practice of using one-off reserves to plug budget gaps; the officer is tightening this off to preserve reserves.
findings.matters: If the council has previously used reserves to mask recurring spending pressures, the stated robustness of the budget is fragile; the officer's conditions suggest this practice must stop, implying stronger discipline will be needed going forward.
findings.figures: No specific numbers; this is a policy condition
findings.quote: Not considering further calls on reserves to meet service growth or recurring expenditure other than for those risks that have been identified, those that could not have been reasonably foreseen and those risks that cannot be dealt with through management or policy actions.

findings.headline: Unallocated reserves now at statutory minimum 10% (£46.7m), down from £63.5m in 2024/25
findings.detail: General Fund unallocated reserves have fallen £16.8m in two years to exactly 10% of net expenditure. The Section 151 Officer cannot recommend below this floor; any further deterioration would breach reserves policy, leaving no headroom for unforeseen costs or savings shortfalls.
findings.matters: A council at its minimum safe reserve level has no buffer; if 2026/27 savings delivery repeats 2025/26's 68% rate, a £10m+ gap would force an emergency draw on reserves, breaching policy and signalling financial distress.
findings.figures: £46.7m unallocated 2026/27 at 10% minimum; down from £63.5m in 2024/25; earmarked reserves £188.3m but allocated for specific purposes
findings.quote: To reflect the challenging operating environment and related financial risks, the Section 151 Officer recommends that the Council maintains a minimum unallocated General Fund balance at a level of at least 10% of net expenditure.

findings.headline: High-risk existing savings commitments concentrated in Adult Social Care (£1.6m) and Finance (£1.6m)
findings.detail: Table 3 shows £4.832m of existing MTFP savings rated high-risk of non-delivery, reflecting that multi-year commitments from prior budgets are proving harder to achieve than expected. Adult Social Care faces £1.628m high-risk existing savings plus £1.5m Target Operating Model savings, a demand-led service now under pressure.
findings.matters: Multi-year savings slippage signals prior-year budget assumptions were optimistic; councils that cannot deliver promised savings struggle with financial control; demand-led services facing savings cuts may face cost spikes if demand rises.
findings.figures: £4.832m high-risk existing savings total; Adult Social Care £1.628m high-risk, £1.5m TOM savings; Children's & Education £1.430m (all high-risk); Finance & Resources £1.564m high-risk
findings.quote: The difficulty in delivering the 2026/27 savings carried forward from previous years naturally provides a higher risk of full delivery in 2026/27. A large proportion of these savings are the second year of the workforce savings, but Adult Social Care also have Target Operating Model savings of £1.5m relating to 2026/27.

findings.headline: Council must deliver £33.3m annual savings, but £12m already missed 2025/26 deadline
findings.detail: Table 4 shows £11.989m of 2025/26 savings targets carried forward to 2026/27 because they were not achieved. The council completed only 68% of 2025/26 savings by Q3. This means the largest-ever annual savings target includes savings already proven difficult to hit, raising execution risk.
findings.matters: A lender needs confidence the council can deliver the savings it depends on; carrying forward misses from the prior year and taking them on again alongside new targets materially increases shortfall risk.
findings.figures: £33.278m 2026/27 total (£11.189m new + £10.100m existing + £11.989m delayed); 68% delivery rate on 2025/26 savings (£13.201m delivered of £39.135m target)
findings.quote: The council also has £12m of delayed savings in 2025/26 – see table 4 below. All savings in 2025/26 that are not delivered were assessed at 50% likelihood of delivery in 2026/27 to account for any future possible delays.

findings.detail: The council notes that 'business rates have gradually increased before flatlining in the last year, due to lower multipliers'. Nottingham's unemployment rate is 2% higher than the national average, indicating underlying local economic weakness.
findings.matters: Business rates flatlining alongside above-average local unemployment signals income risk to the MTFP's key funding sources.

findings.headline: £4.5m contingency provisioned for Integrated Care Board liabilities as negotiations with ICB are still ongoing
findings.detail: The council has budgeted a £10m provision for Adult Social Care joint care packages due to 'reduced funding of joint care packages' from the ICB. The council explicitly states this contingency is 'not expected to fully materialise as negotiations are ongoing', creating budget uncertainty in a material area.
findings.matters: A material budget contingency in a volatile area signals risks that could force mid-year savings if negotiations move against the council.

findings.headline: Social care demand is the primary reason council tax must rise by 3.5% despite Fair Funding II settlement improvement
findings.detail: The council is applying the full 2% Adult Social Care Precept plus an additional 1.5% council tax increase specifically to mitigate social care pressures. The budget report explicitly notes 'continuing social care pressures facing the Council' and cites this as the driver for the maximum council tax rise.
findings.matters: Unrelenting social care demand is the primary reason council tax must rise despite Fair Funding II settlement improvements, signaling that the council's costs are growing faster than core funding.
findings.figures: Total council tax increase 3.5% (1.5% non-social care + 2% social care precept); Band D increases by £79.20 to £2,342.08
findings.quote: In recognition of the continuing social care pressures facing the Council, the 2% Social Care precept flexibility in 2025/26 has been assumed within the budget. In addition, a 1.5% increase in non-social care Council Tax is recommended, leading to a total 3.5% increase in total council tax

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation will cost £28m to be funded from reserves, with no provision in the MTFP
findings.detail: PwC analysis identified £28m required for the council's preferred LGR model, to be funded from the General Fund unallocated balance. The council acknowledges 'transformation costs of this scale are difficult to estimate' and notes these costs are not provided for in the current MTFP, creating unfunded liabilities.
findings.matters: A material reserve drawdown for reorganisation costs will significantly reduce financial resilience at a time when local government is under stress and when the council faces a multi-year structural deficit.
findings.figures: £28m LGR transition costs; General Fund unallocated balance £42.092m at 31 March 2026

findings.headline: £11.989m of savings from 2025/26 were not delivered and are carried forward into 2026/27
findings.detail: The council carried forward undelivered savings of £11.989m from the prior year, representing 53% of the new savings target for 2026/27 (£11.948m). This track record of non-delivery undermines confidence in the council's ability to achieve future savings targets.
findings.matters: A track record of undelivered savings suggests the council's ability to hit future targets is at risk, particularly concerning when the 2026/27 budget depends on delivering £11.948m of new savings.
findings.figures: £11.989m undelivered from 2025/26; £11.948m new savings required for 2026/27
findings.quote: To note the total savings over the MTFP 2026/27 to 2029/30 period are £22.113m before taking account of the undelivered savings of £11.989m carried forward from 2025/26

findings.headline: Cumulative budget gap of £37.1m over four years with no savings identified for 2027/28 to 2029/30
findings.detail: The 2026/27 budget shows a £1.063m surplus, but the council faces a projected cumulative budget gap of £37.107m over the 4-year MTFP without new savings identified for years 2027/28 to 2029/30. The council aspirationally targets £50m in savings (£10m, £20m, £20m across the later years) but these are not yet approved or detailed.
findings.matters: A lender needs confidence that a projected multi-year deficit has a credible delivery plan, but none exists yet for £37m of required savings.
findings.figures: £37.107m cumulative gap; 2026/27 surplus £1.063m; £50m aspirational savings target
findings.quote: Notes that the Council has a projected cumulative budget gap of £37.107m over the 4-year MTFP period without new savings being identified for years 2027/28 to 2029/30

findings.headline: Exceptional Financial Support budgeted to balance 2025/26 but now not required, signalling underlying budget gap
findings.detail: The council's 2025/26 budget was approved incorporating £20.8m of Exceptional Financial Support (financed from capital receipts) to balance the budget. Due to forecast underspends, this is no longer required for this year. However, the baseline budget gap signals structural pressures that remain unresolved in future years' MTFP.
findings.matters: Reliance on EFS and capital receipts to balance budgets is not sustainable; the existence of the gap indicates the council's MTFP contains unresolved funding challenges for future years
findings.figures: £20.8m EFS budgeted; £0m forecast required; £1.6m projected underspend on break-even basis
findings.quote: To note the General Fund budget includes a budget gap of £20.8m which was scheduled to be met through the application of Exceptional Financial Support (EFS), which would be financed through use of capital receipts. However, due to the level of forecasted underspend, the projected EFS of £20.8m is no longer required.

findings.headline: HRA overspend of £1.5m driven by £7.9m provision for damp, mould and legal disrepair works
findings.detail: The Housing Revenue Account is overspending by £1.5m. The main driver is £7.9m of pressures for damp, mould and Legal Disrepair works arising from a stock condition survey and legal disrepair process. These costs were budgeted in the capital programme but are properly chargeable to revenue. HRA reserves will be drawn down to £4.8m contribution, up from the budgeted £3.3m.
findings.matters: The need to charge £7.9m of asset works to revenue signals emerging asset condition risks; growing HRA reserve drawdown reduces financial flexibility and raises questions about the adequacy of the capital programme for asset maintenance
findings.figures: £1.5m HRA overspend; £7.9m damp, mould and disrepair provision; £0.7m void property repair overspend; HRA reserve contribution rising to £4.8m from £3.3m budgeted
findings.quote: £7.9m pressure for damp and mould related HHSRS (Housing, Health & Safety Rating System) and Legal Disrepair works work arising from a stock condition survey and the legal disrepair process. Some of these costs were previously budgeted for in the capital programme. However, these costs are properly chargeable to revenue

findings.headline: DSG High Needs running £7.9m in-year deficit with planned deficits through 2027/28
findings.detail: The Dedicated Schools Grant High Needs service is forecast to run a £7.9m deficit in 2025/26, followed by further deficits in 2026/27 (£3.3m) and 2027/28 (£0.3m). Reserves are being drawn down from £14.6m opening balance to just £3.1m by end of 2027/28. The document notes this 'takes no account of the potential impact of Government's reforms on DSG/SEND provision or Local Government Reorganisation.'
findings.matters: DSG deficits are a statutory concern and signal structural underfunding of SEND provision; continued deficits through the medium term erode reserves and reduce financial flexibility for other pressures
findings.figures: £7.9m 2025/26 deficit; £3.3m 2026/27 deficit; £0.3m 2027/28 deficit; opening reserves £14.6m declining to £3.1m by 2027/28
findings.quote: As per above table, the council expects to run a £7.9m deficit in 2025/26, leading to a residual £6.7m closing reserve balance. After further deficits in 2026/27 and 2027/28, it anticipates moving back in-year surpluses.

findings.headline: Adults and Public Health overspend of £13.1m driven by external care demand and undelivered savings
findings.detail: The directorate is overspending by £13.1m against a £90.1m budget, with external care packages overspending by £4.5m across all service user groups (older people £1.8m, physical disability £2.3m, learning disabilities £0.6m). The service is delivering only 53% of its £10.7m savings target. The document identifies this as structural, driven by rising demand and increasing complexity of citizen needs.
findings.matters: Adult social care represents material budget impact and pressures are structural rather than one-off; rising care package volumes (10,307 total) indicate demand is growing, not stabilising
findings.figures: £13.1m overspend; £4.5m external care package overspend; 10,307 total care packages (3,560 older people, 2,731 learning disabilities, 2,465 physical disability, 1,551 mental health); only £5.7m of £10.7m savings forecast to be delivered in-year
findings.quote: Adult Social Care is experiencing significant budgetary and capacity pressures, impacting its ability to meet the rising demand for services. This is driven by an ageing population and the increasing complexity of citizen needs.

findings.headline: Only 68% of £39.1m savings target expected to be delivered in-year, with £12.4m not expected to be delivered
findings.detail: The council targeted £39.1m of savings for 2025/26 but now forecasts delivering only £26.7m (68%). Of the undelivered amount, £12m is delayed to 2026/27 and £5.1m represents non-delivery. The council is mitigating the shortfall with over £10m of staffing vacancies, which is not a sustainable strategy.
findings.matters: Savings miss of this scale indicates budget assumptions are fragile; reliance on vacancy management is not a reliable mitigation and leaves the council exposed if recruitment proceeds as planned
findings.figures: £39.1m savings target; £26.7m (68%) forecast to be delivered; £12m delayed to 2026/27; £5.1m non-delivered; £10m+ staffing vacancies relied upon as mitigation
findings.quote: The council forecasts to achieve £26.7m out of £39.1m in savings in 2025/26, which means that £12.4m is not expected to be delivered and the forecast relies on mitigations, including over £10m of staffing vacancies.

findings.headline: £9m provision for integrated care board reduction in jointly funded care placement funding
findings.detail: The council is recognising a £9m worst-case provision for potential reductions in ICB funding for jointly funded care packages. The document explicitly states this is 'not an acceptance of liability' and that 'dispute resolution is ongoing', but the council is adopting a 'prudent approach' and provisioning at the conservative end of the spectrum due to year-end proximity.
findings.matters: This is a contingent liability that could worsen if the dispute proceeds unfavourably; it represents a structural change in how jointly funded care is financed that will affect future years regardless of dispute outcome
findings.figures: £9m provision in 2025/26; £9m income shortfall in Mental Health and Whole Life Disability service; total external care package overspend of £4.5m
findings.quote: Within this overspend the council is prudently recognising a £9m provision in relation to the potential reduction of income due to the new ICB approach in relation to jointly funded care placements. This provision represents the worst-case scenario and is not an acceptance of liability and dispute resolution is ongoing

findings.headline: 40.6% of remaining debt matures in 25–40 years, creating a refinancing wall around 2050–2065 that current financial strategy does not yet address.
findings.detail: Table 15 shows maturity structure. The upper threshold for borrowing maturing in the 25–40 year bucket is 40.6% of debt. Section 1.15 notes 'the Council reviewed its maturity thresholds accordingly' after the £300m+ reduction, but the concentration in this mid-range maturity bucket means a significant wall of loans will need refinancing simultaneously in ~30 years' time. Section 6.19 acknowledges the importance: 'this matters because it is important to ensure that the council does not re-finance too much of its portfolio.'
findings.matters: Maturity concentration creates refinancing risk. If interest rates are elevated or credit markets are tight in 2050–2065, the council may face forced repricing of 40% of its debt base at once. Long-term fiscal planning should address this, but current strategy focuses on shorter-term reserve management.
findings.figures: 40.6% of debt matures 25–40 years hence; 24.4% matures 10–25 years; only 7.1% under 5 years
findings.quote: the upper threshold for borrowing maturing within 25 to 40 years now represents 40.6% of its debt

findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account debt-to-revenues ratio at 114% for 2025/26 (declining only to 82% by 2029/30) signals constrained housing investment capacity.
findings.detail: Table 13 shows HRA debt of £148.9m against revenues of £130.3m (2025/26), implying the HRA borrows roughly its own annual income in debt service and capital needs. While improving, 82% debt-to-revenues (2029/30) leaves little room for expansion or new supply. The HRA is highly geared and any deterioration in rental income or increase in repairs costs could be problematic.
findings.matters: HRA debt is secured on housing assets and tenants' rents. High leverage constrains the council's ability to respond to housing need, including affordable housing supply. For a lender, high HRA gearing suggests limited flexibility and concentration risk in a single service.
findings.figures: HRA debt £148.9m (2025/26); HRA revenues £130.3m; ratio 114.25%; declining to 82.06% by 2029/30
findings.quote: Debt (£m)  148.855  Revenues (£m) 130.290  Ratio of Debt to Revenues (%) 114.25%

findings.headline: Commercial property investment portfolio of £212.1m (mostly borrowed) earning only £9.3m net income; council actively seeking to divest.
findings.detail: Table 24 lists 18+ commercial projects (dubbed Project Doncaster, Project Mulberry, etc.) totalling £212.1m purchase price, of which £208.1m was financed by borrowing. Section 10.5 states 'The Council regularly reviews its investments to identify opportunities for divestment, helping to reduce debt more quickly and support delivery of the Voluntary Debt Reduction policy.' The low net income (£9.334m forecast for 2025/26) suggests either underperforming assets or heavy depreciation charges. No new commercial investments permitted.
findings.matters: If these regeneration/property assets are underperforming, forced sales to raise cash could occur at cyclical lows. Fire-sale asset disposals typically signal financial distress. A lender needs to know whether the £212m is performing, whether write-downs are likely, and whether the council has flexibility to hold underperforming assets through cycles.
findings.figures: £212.1m commercial investments; £208.1m financed by borrowing; £9.334m forecast net income 2025/26; no new commercial investments permitted
findings.quote: The Council regularly reviews its investments to identify opportunities for divestment, helping to reduce debt more quickly and support delivery of the Voluntary Debt Reduction policy.

findings.headline: Capital spending rationed to £52m by 2029/30 (down 74% from current levels) because no new borrowing is permitted except in emergencies.
findings.detail: The Voluntary Debt Reduction Policy from section 12.3 states: 'For the period 2025/26 to 2029/30, no new schemes are to be financed by borrowing.' Table 1 shows capital programme collapsing from £199.6m (2024/25 actual) to £52.4m (2029/30 est). This constraint is independent of project merit or service need.
findings.matters: A five-year capital freeze signals the council is managing cash-flow distress, not strategic choice. Underfunded capital creates deferred maintenance, equipment obsolescence, and service degradation that eventually cost more to fix. For regeneration and economic development, it signals retreat.
findings.figures: Capital spending: £199.6m (2024/25) down to £52.4m (2029/30); no new borrowing permitted 2025/26-2029/30
findings.quote: For the period 2025/26 to 2029/30, no new schemes are to be financed by borrowing.

findings.headline: Council repaid £287m of debt in 2025/26 and is now drawing down reserves to fund the under-borrowed position—expected to hit negative investment balances by 2027/28.
findings.detail: The council undertook two large debt repayments: £89m in August 2025 and £198m in December 2025, reducing gross debt from £741.8m to £435.7m in a single year. Table 5 shows expected investments declining from £351.1m (actual 2024/25) to £109.9m (2025/26 est) to negative £26.1m by 2027/28, meaning the council will need to borrow to meet normal operations unless reserves can be supplemented by asset sales.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know the council's cash runway and whether this aggressive strategy is sustainable. Once reserves hit limits, the no-new-borrowing policy may need to break, or the council may be forced to cut services or sell assets at disadvantageous times.
findings.figures: £287m debt repayment in 2025/26; usable reserves projected to fall from £456.9m (2024/25) to £317.8m (2028/29); expected investments turning negative (negative £26.1m by 2027/28)
findings.quote: The Council is currently under‑borrowed, meaning it is using its own cash (reserves and working capital) instead of taking out new loans. No new General Fund or Housing Revenue Account borrowing is expected during the forecast period.

findings.headline: £212m commercial property portfolio generates £10.6m annual revenue but exposed to market downturn
findings.detail: Commercial property investments total £212m (purchase price), capital value £200.554m at 31 March 2025, funded by £208m of unsupported borrowing. These generate £10.552m net annual revenue to the General Fund (4.52% yield). The council explicitly acknowledges exposure to market risks including downturns, voids, lease breaks and wider economic pressures. Asset sales planned for 2026/27 to reduce debt.
findings.matters: General Fund revenue budget is materially dependent on £10.6m annual yield from properties; any market downturn, vacancy spike, or lease break would directly squeeze budget balance and debt reduction targets.

findings.quote: The gross investment of £222.812m (excluding MRP to 31 March 2025) exposes the Council to market risks such as downturns, voids, lease breaks and wider economic pressures.

findings.headline: £19m essential asset maintenance backlog added to capital programme
findings.detail: The capital programme includes £19m of urgent works to address core fabric issues in council-owned assets. The council explicitly describes these as non-transformational works aimed solely at preventing further asset deterioration, not enhancing value or performance.
findings.matters: Allocation signals underlying condition problems in the council estate; deferring these works would lead to accelerating deterioration costs and potential service disruption.
findings.figures: £19m allocated to urgent maintenance works in current programme
findings.quote: The Capital Programme includes £19m of urgent works to address core fabric issues in Council assets, preventing higher future costs if delayed. These works are not transformational and do not enhance building value or performance; they simply prevent further deterioration.

findings.headline: £37.5m of approved capital schemes removed from programme due to lack of funding
findings.detail: Pipeline schemes totalling £37.502m have been reclassified as temporarily decommissioned and placed outside the capital programme due to unavailable funding. The council acknowledges risks relating to these unfunded schemes are escalating with potential knock-on implications for service delivery.
findings.matters: Service delivery risks are acknowledged as increasing; council cannot fund schemes it identifies as necessary, signalling financial constraint is worse than headline figures suggest.
findings.figures: £37.502m in decommissioned/pipeline schemes
findings.quote: It is recognised that the risks of not incorporating these schemes into the Capital Programme are increasing and may have knock on implications for service delivery.

findings.headline: Council must generate £28.4m from asset sales to fund its approved capital programme
findings.detail: The five-year capital programme (2025/26–2029/30) requires £81.167m of capital receipts. While £52.744m is already available, the council must generate an additional £28.423m through property disposals. This creates material execution risk: if property sales slip or property values fall short, capital schemes will require deferral or cancellation.
findings.matters: Capital programme delivery depends entirely on meeting asset sales targets at sufficient values; shortfalls will force service cuts or project delays.
findings.figures: £81.167m capital receipts required, £52.744m available, £28.423m shortfall
findings.quote: The current capital programme requires £81.167m of capital receipts. £52.744m are already available in 2025/26 and it needs to generate £28.423m more to fill the gap.

findings.headline: Capital borrowing prohibition continues beyond 2026/27 despite end of government support
findings.detail: Council issued a Section 114 report in November 2023 due to budget imbalance and received Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) for 2023/24 and 2024/25 with an associated prohibition on capital borrowing. Although the EFS requirement ends in 2026/27, the borrowing prohibition will remain while the council strengthens its financial position.
findings.matters: Even as crisis support ends, the council remains unable to borrow for capital investment, forcing reliance on a fully-funded capital programme and eliminating growth options.
findings.figures: EFS received 2023/24 to 2024/25; prohibition continues indefinitely
findings.quote: In 2026/27, the requirement for EFS has ended but the prohibition remains, while the council strengthens its financial position.

findings.headline: Children's services carries prior-year £4.4m overspend while transformation programme started in April 2025; Ofsted rated Inadequate in 2022
findings.detail: Children's & Education is forecasting £1.6m overspend but this sits on top of a £4.4m prior-year overspend that remains outstanding. The transformation programme started from scratch in April 2025. Children's Regulatory Services alone is overspending by £3.0m. The service received an Ofsted Inadequate rating in 2022; next full inspection is anticipated in 2025. External placement market risks include higher costs and shortage of suitable placements.
findings.matters: An Ofsted Inadequate rating is a governance red flag. The prior-year overspend plus current pressures plus a transformation programme that has only just begun suggests fundamental management capacity issues. External inspection is imminent.
findings.figures: £1.6m current overspend; £4.4m prior-year overspend; £3.0m Children's Regulatory Services overspend; Ofsted rated Inadequate 2022
findings.quote: This reflects a directorate that started its transformation programme from a standing start in April 2025, and an overhanging prior year overspend of £4.4m.

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant forecasting £4.5m annual deficit with reserve falling to £8.9m after DfE funding cut
findings.detail: DSG is forecasting a £4.5m deficit for 2025/26. The DfE has just announced a £2.7m reduction in the High Needs Allocation (based on lower Published Admission Numbers), leaving a closing reserve of only £8.9m. A full DSG Recovery Plan is being brought forward but has not yet been approved. At the current deficit rate, the reserve will be exhausted in two years.
findings.matters: This is a structural High Needs Block deficit, not a temporary variance. Reserves are the only buffer; they are finite. The DfE has just cut funding, not increased it.
findings.figures: £4.5m annual deficit; £8.9m closing reserve (down from £16.0m opening); £2.7m DfE funding reduction
findings.quote: The DSG contained within the Children's & Education Directorate is forecasting a deficit of £4.5m for 2025/26 with an estimated closing reserve balance of £8.9m.

findings.headline: Adult Social Care is £3.9m (4.1%) over budget with rising external care costs and demand-driven structural pressures
findings.detail: ASC overspend is across external care: Learning Disabilities £1.2m, Mental Health £0.4m, Physical Disability £0.9m, Older People £0.5m. Additionally there is a £2.4m shortfall on Continuing Care and client contributions. The report states the directorate is "experiencing significant budgetary and capacity pressures" driven by "an ageing population and the increasing complexity of citizen needs." Risks flagged include National Living Wage rises, inflationary pressures, and provider exits shrinking market capacity.
findings.matters: This is not a one-off variance but a structural demand issue tied to demographics. The aging population will not reverse. External care price inflation and market tightness are accelerating, not temporary.
findings.figures: £3.9m overspend (4.1% of £94.0m budget); external care overspends £3.1m total
findings.quote: Adult Social Care is experiencing significant budgetary and capacity pressures, impacting its ability to meet the rising demand for services. This is driven by an ageing population and the increasing complexity of citizen needs.

findings.headline: £12.4m of the £39.1m savings target (32%) is not expected to be delivered in-year or at all
findings.detail: The budget was built on £39.1m savings, but only £26.7m (68%) is forecast to be delivered. Of the shortfall, £12.2m is delayed and £5.1m is red-flagged as non-delivery. The reported underspend masks this gap with over £10m of staffing vacancies and 'mitigations', creating an unsustainable reliance on holding posts open.
findings.matters: Vacancies cannot provide permanent cover for structural savings failure. When posts are filled, the £10m+ gap will reappear. This suggests either the savings plans were unachievable or delivery governance is weak.

findings.headline: £7.0m emerging liability for damp and mould repairs in council housing stock, up £4.5m from Q1

These costs are properly chargeable to revenue and will force additional draw-down of HRA reserves.

news_drafts.headline: Nottingham auditors unable to approve accounts due to control environment weaknesses
news_drafts.lead: Nottingham City Council's auditors will issue a disclaimer of opinion — meaning they cannot express a view on whether the council's financial statements are fairly presented. The finding, from Grant Thornton, stems from historic weaknesses in the control environment, identified after a breach of the housing revenue account (the separate, ring-fenced account for the council's own housing) in earlier years. These underlying issues remain a factor in the audit risk assessment. The council is working through a formal multi-year Regaining Assurance programme with government oversight. The audit has been hampered by delays: the finance team prioritised meeting the statutory deadline for publishing draft accounts over providing information to auditors, pushing back interim audit work. Despite the challenges, the audit is progressing further than at the equivalent stage last year. Grant Thornton will complete its report by 30 November.
news_drafts.paper_title: Progress report and interim audit findings - September 2026 - AC

news_drafts.headline: Nottingham City loses financial buffer in shared services partnership
news_drafts.lead: The East Midlands Shared Services partnership, which Nottingham City Council funds with £3.2 million a year, has exhausted its financial reserves. The Joint Committee approved the removal of reserves in June 2022 when they fell below best practice levels, and the balance is now entirely depleted. The partnership, which provides services jointly with Leicestershire County Council on a 50-50 basis, previously held reserves to cover redundancy costs and unexpected operational demands. Without this cushion, any overspend in the partnership's £5.8 million annual budget must now be split equally between the two councils. Nottingham City has no contingency to absorb its share of any shortfall.

editorial.headline: Nottingham City audit opinion disclaimed as joint venture reserves depleted
editorial.standfirst: Depleted reserves in a 50:50 partnership and governance weaknesses have left the council without financial buffer or clean audit bill.
editorial.body:
Nottingham City Council faces a compounding set of financial and governance pressures that have left it without the reserves to absorb further shocks.

The council is a 50:50 partner in East Midlands Shared Services. As of 31 March 2026, EMSS reserves were fully depleted. The council's papers presented to June's joint committee meeting state: "The balance of reserve has now been fully depleted and partners will be expected to fund any operational overspend arising in year on a 50:50 basis." This leaves Nottingham City liable for half of any cost overrun.

A month later, Grant Thornton, the council's external auditor, issued a disclaimed audit opinion on the 2025/26 accounts—a rare step indicating it cannot form a view on the reliability of the financial statements. The council's papers presented to July's corporate scrutiny committee describe the work underway: "Council works closely with the External Auditor to identify the key information and evidential requirements that the auditor will need to provide a positive non-qualified audit opinion from a standard base disclaimed opinion."

But internal audit tells a deeper story. As of 31 July, the Head of Internal Audit's annual opinion for 2025/26 provides only Moderate Assurance. The audit committee papers state: "Governance and control improvements are not yet consistently embedded across all areas." Multiple service areas remain problematic. The papers identify Adult Social Care performance and statutory compliance as an ongoing governance issue. Children's Services and Housing Services require continued improvement. Workforce capacity and resilience are constrained.

Compounding these issues is a pay award pressure. The council budgeted 3.5%, but the employers' current offer stands at 3.2%. The EMSS papers note: "Early indications suggest this offer will be rejected, with negotiations ongoing. Consequently, there remains a risk that the final award may be higher than the provision made in the budget for 2026/27."

The combination—zero reserves, audit failure, governance weaknesses not yet embedded—leaves little room for manoeuvre if budget pressures intensify.
editorial.pull_quote: Governance and control improvements are not yet consistently embedded across all areas
editorial.watch_next: Grant Thornton is targeting a non-qualified audit opinion by March 2028, when the council's remediation efforts must demonstrate concrete results.
